All configuration options for the DoctrineProvider This page covers all configuration options for the DoctrineProvider.

<?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Configuration; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => '', 'table_suffix' => '_audit', 'ignored_columns' => [], 'entities' => [], 'viewer' => true, 'storage_mapper' => null, 'utf8_convert' => false, 'full_snapshot_on_remove' => false, 'mask_secret' => null, 'batch_size' => 0, 'skip_disabled_entities' => false, 'compression' => false, 'ignored_columns_resolver' => null, 'root_resolver' => null, 'entity_label_resolver' => null, 'read_scope' => null, ]);

Option Type Default Description table_prefix string '' Prefix for audit table names table_suffix string '_audit' Suffix for audit table names ignored_columns array [] Properties to ignore globally across all entities entities array [] Entity-specific configuration viewer bool|array true Enable/configure the audit viewer storage_mapper callable|class-string|null null Callback, or class name of an invokable class without constructor arguments, routing audits to storage services utf8_convert bool false Convert string values to UTF-8 before storing full_snapshot_on_remove bool false Record every audited field of a removed entity (see below) mask_secret string|null null Secret of the #[Mask(strategy: MaskStrategy::KeyedHash)] fields, at least 32 bytes (see below) batch_size int (≥ 0) 0 Write audit entries with multi-row INSERTs (see Batch INSERT below) skip_disabled_entities bool false No audit table for entities disabled by their configuration (see below) compression bool false Store diffs/extra_data compressed (MariaDB) ignored_columns_resolver callable|null null Returns the properties to ignore for a given entity object (see below) root_resolver callable|null null Returns extra audit roots of an entity object (see Histories) entity_label_resolver callable|null null Builds the label of an entity written in the diffs (see Histories) read_scope callable|null null Applied to every query the reader creates, to restrict what can be read (see Histories)
Audit tables are named based on the original entity table name with optional prefix and suffix: [table_prefix] + [entity_table_name] + [table_suffix]

// Default: posts → posts_audit $configuration = new Configuration([ 'table_suffix' => '_audit', ]); // Custom prefix: posts → audit_posts $configuration = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => 'audit_', 'table_suffix' => '', ]); // Both: posts → audit_posts_log $configuration = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => 'audit_', 'table_suffix' => '_log', ]);
NOTE ignored_columns expects mapped PHP property names (e.g. createdAt), not SQL column names (e.g. created_at). A column name that differs from its property name is silently not ignored.
Properties that should never be audited across all entities: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'ignored_columns' => [ 'createdAt', 'updatedAt', ], ]);

Ignore additional properties for specific entities (combined with the global list): $configuration = new Configuration([ 'entities' => [ App\Entity\User::class => [ 'ignored_columns' => ['password', 'salt'], ], ], ]);

When only a few properties of an entity matter, list them with audited_columns instead of ignoring all the others: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'entities' => [ App\Entity\Order::class => [ 'audited_columns' => ['status', 'total', 'customer'], ], ], ]); Only the listed properties (fields and to-one associations) appear in the diffs; an update that only changes other properties writes no audit entry. Inserts and removals are still audited. null or no audited_columns (the default) audits every property; [] audits no property, so only inserts and removals are recorded (with empty diffs, or the allowlisted properties with full_snapshot_on_remove). The identifier is not audited as a field unless it is listed, but every entry still records it (object_id and the diff source). An allowlist cannot audit an ignored property: global and per-entity ignored_columns, #[Ignore] and the ignored_columns_resolver always win (see Which properties are audited).

ignored_columns and audited_columns apply to every object of an entity class. To decide per object (e.g. skip a field while a document is a draft), give ignored_columns_resolver a callable that receives the entity object and returns the properties to ignore for it: use App\Entity\Document; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\IgnoredColumnsResolverInterface; final class DocumentIgnoredColumnsResolver implements IgnoredColumnsResolverInterface { public function __invoke(object $entity): array { if ($entity instanceof Document && $entity->isDraft()) { return ['content']; } return []; } } $configuration = new Configuration([ 'ignored_columns_resolver' => new DocumentIgnoredColumnsResolver(), ]); // or later, with any callable (null removes it) $configuration->setIgnoredColumnsResolver(static fn (object $entity): array => []); The resolver is called for every audited entity object, once per insert, update and (with full_snapshot_on_remove) removal, with the entity as it is when the flush is processed: keep it cheap. It must return a list of property names; anything else throws an UnexpectedValueException. Its result is added to the ignored properties: a resolver can ignore more properties, never audit a property that the configuration ignores or leaves out of audited_columns. isAuditedField() applies it when given an entity object, not a class name.

A property is audited when its entity is audited and the property is: not in the global ignored_columns, not in the entity ignored_columns nor marked with #[Ignore], listed in the entity audited_columns, when the entity has one, not returned by the ignored_columns_resolver for that object, when one is set. Ignoring always wins: a property listed in audited_columns but ignored by any other rule is not audited. NOTE These rules apply to fields and to-one associations, which are recorded in the diffs. Changes of to-many associations are recorded as associate / dissociate entries and are not filtered by property.

Configure entities programmatically instead of (or in addition to) using attributes: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'entities' => [ App\Entity\User::class => [ 'enabled' => true, 'ignored_columns' => ['password', 'salt'], 'roles' => [ 'view' => ['ROLE_ADMIN'], // Who can view these audits ], ], App\Entity\Post::class => [ 'enabled' => true, ], App\Entity\Draft::class => [ 'enabled' => false, // Disabled even if has #[Auditable] ], ], ]);

Option Type Default Description enabled bool true Whether auditing is enabled for this entity ignored_columns array [] Properties to ignore for this entity audited_columns ?array null Allowlist: only these properties are audited (null: all) roles array null View permissions (['view' => ['ROLE_X']]) max_age ?string null Retention: ISO 8601 duration applied by audit:clean instead of the global cutoff max_entries ?int null Retention: number of most recent entries kept by audit:clean roots list<string> [] Audit root paths, merged with #[AuditRoot] (see Histories) max_age and max_entries take precedence over the #[Auditable(maxAge: ..., maxEntries: ...)] values, key by key: setting only max_age keeps the attribute maxEntries, and an explicit null disables the attribute value. They are validated (positive ISO 8601 duration, positive integer) before audit:clean deletes anything. For an entity marked #[Auditable], the configured options combine with the attributes: enabled: false disables the entity despite #[Auditable]; enabled: true does not re-enable an #[Auditable(enabled: false)] entity. roles take precedence over #[Security], scope by scope (view): roles: null, an empty array or a missing view key keeps the attribute value. ignored_columns and roots are added to the #[Ignore] and #[AuditRoot] ones; audited_columns only exists in the configuration.

The viewer option controls the built-in audit viewer (when integrated with a UI layer): // Enable with defaults $configuration = new Configuration([ 'viewer' => true, ]); // Disable $configuration = new Configuration([ 'viewer' => false, ]); // Custom page size $configuration = new Configuration([ 'viewer' => [ 'enabled' => true, 'page_size' => 25, // Default is 50 ], ]);

The utf8_convert option ensures string values are converted to valid UTF-8 before being stored in the diffs JSON column. Useful when your database or entities may contain non-UTF-8 encoded data: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'utf8_convert' => true, ]);

By default, a remove entry only identifies the deleted entity: its diff holds the source block (id, class, label, table) and an empty changes. With full_snapshot_on_remove, it also records the value of every audited field before the deletion, as old (with new set to null), so that the last state of a deleted entity can be read from its audit history. A generated identifier is left out of these fields, as in an insert entry: Doctrine resets it on deletion, and the source block holds it. The owning-side to-one associations (ManyToOne, owning OneToOne) are recorded as in an insert entry, with the summary of their target (id, class, label, table) as old; a null association is left out, and so are to-many associations. The targets that are not loaded yet are loaded with one query per target class, and a target deleted in the same flush keeps the identifier it had before the deletion. $configuration = new Configuration([ 'full_snapshot_on_remove' => true, ]); The snapshot makes remove entries larger, and lets ChangedFieldFilter match them on any of their fields.

mask_secret keys the HMAC-SHA256 that #[Mask(strategy: MaskStrategy::KeyedHash)] stores instead of a value (see Attributes). It must be at least 32 bytes long. Without it, an entity with a keyed hash mask fails when the attributes are loaded. $configuration = new Configuration([ 'mask_secret' => $_ENV['AUDIT_MASK_SECRET'], ]); Changing the secret changes the hashes of the values recorded from then on: the entries recorded before can no longer be matched with the new ones.

By default (batch_size: 0), each audit entry is written with its own INSERT statement as soon as it is produced. A positive batch_size buffers the audit entries of the database transaction being committed and writes them with multi-row INSERT statements, which saves round trips to the database when a transaction changes many entities: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'batch_size' => 500, ]); TIP With 500 to 1,000 audited entities per flush, batch_size: 500 made a flush 10 to 18 % faster on SQLite, 19 to 51 % faster on MySQL and 44 to 67 % faster on PostgreSQL in our measurements: see Performance for the method, the full results and how to reproduce them. Why is it off by default? Only because of the id: a LifecycleEvent listener, or another storage provider, that reads $payload['id'] gets no id from a buffered entry (see below). If nothing in your application reads it, a positive batch_size is the largest speed-up available for flushes of many entities, and turning it on changes nothing else: the entries are written in the same database transaction, and a failure still fails the commit. You read $payload['id'] in a listener or another provider? Recommended batch_size No 500 Yes 0 (default): the id is set When: the buffered audit entries are written right before the COMMIT of the audited transaction, or as soon as batch_size entries are buffered. Values between 100 and 1000 are a good start: the larger the value, the fewer statements, but the more memory the buffer holds for a large transaction. Per-statement limit: whatever batch_size, a single statement holds at most 99 rows on SQLite (bound parameter limit of older SQLite versions) and 500 rows on MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL. Other platforms are limited to 99 rows per statement and must support the multi-row INSERT INTO … VALUES (…), (…) syntax. A statement is also closed before its string values (diffs, extra data, blame…) exceed 1 MiB, a larger audit entry being written alone: MySQL and MariaDB reject a statement larger than their max_allowed_packet setting (64 MiB by default since MySQL 8.0, as low as 1 MiB on older or tuned servers). Keep max_allowed_packet comfortably above 1 MiB, and above the size of your largest audit entry (as with batch_size: 0). No id in the payload: the LifecycleEvent payload of a buffered audit entry has no id key, since the entry is not written yet when it is persisted. With batch_size: 0, the provider adds the id of the inserted row to the payload once the entry is written (on PostgreSQL, through INSERT … RETURNING id, in the same round trip). Failures fail the commit: if an audit entry cannot be buffered (e.g. the storage mapper throws) or the buffered audit entries cannot be written, the commit fails with the first of these failures and the audited transaction is rolled back, so that no change is committed without its audit entries (as with batch_size: 0, where a failure to write an audit entry also fails the flush). This includes audit entries stored on another connection (see Multi-Database Configuration): those already written by an early batch are deleted when the audited transaction is rolled back, as they are with batch_size: 0. Outside of a commit: DoctrineProvider::persist() called directly, outside of the commit of an audited transaction, still writes the audit entry immediately.

On MySQL and MariaDB, audit tables can become the largest tables of a database: almost all of their size is the diffs column (and extra_data when used). The compression option stores these two columns compressed: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'compression' => true, ]); Platform Effect MariaDB diffs and extra_data are declared JSON COMPRESSED (transparent column compression) PostgreSQL None: large JSONB values are already compressed by PostgreSQL (TOAST) MySQL None: MySQL has no column compression (see Schema Management) SQLite None MariaDB compresses and decompresses the values transparently: reading audit entries, JsonFilter and JSON functions in SQL work unchanged. Values shorter than column_compression_threshold (100 bytes by default) are stored as is. Compression trades CPU for disk space and I/O. Reading a large history whose pages are already in memory gets slower, since every value has to be decompressed: in the contributor's measurements (34,279 audit rows, MariaDB 11.8), reading an entity with ~510 changes took 16.0 ms instead of 7.5 ms (median, warm cache). Reads that hit the disk get faster (59.8 ms instead of 138.6 ms, cold cache) and writes are not slower, since there is much less data to read and write. New audit tables are created with compressed columns. Existing audit tables are converted by audit:schema:update --force (or by a migration containing the SQL shown by audit:schema:update --dump-sql): altering the columns rewrites the table and compresses existing entries. Disabling the option and running audit:schema:update again converts the columns back, without losing data. NOTE The schema comparator of Doctrine DBAL does not see the COMPRESSED attribute, so doctrine:schema:update and doctrine:migrations:diff neither report nor change the compression of existing audit tables: use audit:schema:update for that. Conversely, they never report a difference for compressed columns. WARNING Converting existing tables rewrites them (ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY), which takes time on large tables. Before MariaDB 11.2, writes to the audit table are also locked for the duration of the rewrite, so audited flushes wait for it; since MariaDB 11.2, the rewrite runs online by default (ALGORITHM=COPY, LOCK=NONE). Plan it like any other large schema migration.

An entity disabled by its configuration (#[Auditable(enabled: false)], or 'enabled' => false, also on an #[Auditable] entity) is not audited, but it still gets an audit table: auditing can be enabled for it at runtime with enableAuditFor(), and the audit entries need somewhere to go. When you never enable such entities at runtime, skip_disabled_entities leaves them without an audit table: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'skip_disabled_entities' => true, ]); audit:schema:update, doctrine:schema:update and doctrine:migrations:diff all skip these entities, so the result does not depend on the tool that manages your schema. Existing audit tables of these entities are left as they are: drop them yourself if you no longer need them. enableAuditFor() throws a LogicException for these entities, instead of a failing flush later on. Entities enabled by their configuration and disabled at runtime with disableAuditFor() keep their audit table. The Reader refuses to query these entities and ignores them when reading a transaction. Entities configured without an enabled key are enabled, so they are never skipped.

When using multiple storage EntityManagers, the storage mapper determines where to store audits for each entity. NOTE See Multi-Database Configuration for detailed information. use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'storage_mapper' => function (string $entity, array $storageServices): StorageService { // Route User audits to a dedicated storage if ($entity === App\Entity\User::class) { return $storageServices['users_audit_storage']; } // Default storage for everything else return $storageServices['default']; }, ]);

// Check if an entity class is configured for auditing $provider->isAuditable(App\Entity\Post::class); // bool // Check if auditing is currently active (respects enabled flag) $provider->isAudited(App\Entity\Post::class); // bool // Check if a specific field is being audited $provider->isAuditedField(App\Entity\Post::class, 'title'); // true $provider->isAuditedField(App\Entity\Post::class, 'password'); // false (if ignored)

TIP Configuration from PHP attributes and programmatic config are merged intelligently. PHP attributes on entities are loaded first (via AttributeLoader): for an entity with #[Auditable], they provide enabled, roles (#[Security]) and the #[Ignore] properties enabled: false in the programmatic configuration disables the entity despite #[Auditable] (enabled: true cannot re-enable an #[Auditable(enabled: false)] entity), and its roles take precedence over #[Security], scope by scope The entity ignored_columns and roots of the programmatic configuration are added to the #[Ignore] properties and #[AuditRoot] paths The entity audited_columns and the retention options (max_age, max_entries, key by key) of the programmatic configuration are kept Global ignored_columns and the ignored_columns_resolver apply on top of the entity options // Given this entity with attributes: #[Auditable] #[Security(view: ['ROLE_USER'])] class Post { #[Ignore] private string $cached = ''; } // And this programmatic config: $configuration = new Configuration([ 'ignored_columns' => ['updatedAt'], 'entities' => [ Post::class => [ 'ignored_columns' => ['slug'], 'audited_columns' => ['title', 'slug', 'cached', 'updatedAt'], ], ], ]); // Final configuration for Post: // - entity ignored_columns: ['cached', 'slug'] (+ the global 'updatedAt') // - audited_columns: ['title', 'slug', 'cached', 'updatedAt'] => only 'title' is audited // - roles: ['view' => ['ROLE_USER']]

<?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Configuration; use App\Entity\{User, Post, Comment, Order, Payment}; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => '', 'table_suffix' => '_audit', 'ignored_columns' => [ 'createdAt', 'updatedAt', ], 'entities' => [ User::class => [ 'enabled' => true, 'ignored_columns' => ['password', 'salt'], 'roles' => ['view' => ['ROLE_ADMIN']], ], Post::class => [ 'enabled' => true, ], Comment::class => [ 'enabled' => true, 'roles' => ['view' => ['ROLE_MODERATOR', 'ROLE_ADMIN']], ], Order::class => [ 'enabled' => true, ], Payment::class => [ 'enabled' => true, 'roles' => ['view' => ['ROLE_ACCOUNTANT', 'ROLE_ADMIN']], ], ], 'viewer' => [ 'enabled' => true, 'page_size' => 50, ], 'storage_mapper' => null, // Single database, no mapper needed 'compression' => true, // MariaDB only, ignored on other platforms ]);

Store audit entries in a separate database This guide explains how to configure the DoctrineProvider to store audit entries in a dedicated database, separate from your application database.

There are several reasons to store audits in a separate database: Performance isolation — Heavy audit write traffic doesn't affect your application DB Security — Restrict access to audit data independently from application data Retention policies — Apply different backup and archiving strategies to audits Compliance — Keep audit data in a separate system with stricter access controls

Multi-database setups involve: One (or more) AuditingService(s) wrapping the application EntityManager(s) (source of events) One (or more) StorageService(s) wrapping the audit EntityManager(s) A storage_mapper callback to route each entity's audits to the right storage service (required when more than one StorageService is registered)

Set up two EntityManagers: one for your application, one for the audit database. <?php // $appEntityManager → reads/writes your application entities // $auditEntityManager → writes audit rows to a separate database IMPORTANT The connection of the application EntityManager (the auditing one) must be created with the AuditorMiddleware (see the Quick Start): the audit entries are written when its transaction is committed.

Since there is only one storage service, no storage mapper is needed — all audits go to 'audit' automatically: <?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Configuration; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\DoctrineProvider; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'table_suffix' => '_audit', 'entities' => [ App\Entity\User::class => ['enabled' => true], App\Entity\Post::class => ['enabled' => true], ], // No storage_mapper needed when there is only one StorageService ]); $provider = new DoctrineProvider($configuration);

<?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService; $provider->registerAuditingService( new AuditingService('app', $appEntityManager) ); $provider->registerStorageService( new StorageService('audit', $auditEntityManager) );
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Schema\SchemaManager; (new SchemaManager($provider))->updateAuditSchema(); // Creates tables in the audit EntityManager's database

When you need different entities routed to different storage services: <?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Configuration; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\DoctrineProvider; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'entities' => [ App\Entity\User::class => ['enabled' => true], App\Entity\Payment::class => ['enabled' => true], App\Entity\Post::class => ['enabled' => true], ], // Required when more than one StorageService is registered 'storage_mapper' => function (string $entity, array $storageServices): StorageService { return match ($entity) { App\Entity\User::class, App\Entity\Payment::class => $storageServices['audit_sensitive'], default => $storageServices['audit_general'], }; }, ]); $provider = new DoctrineProvider($configuration); // Register the auditing service (application EntityManager) $provider->registerAuditingService( new AuditingService('app', $appEntityManager) ); // Register multiple storage services, keyed by name in $storageServices $provider->registerStorageService( new StorageService('audit_sensitive', $auditSensitiveEntityManager) ); $provider->registerStorageService( new StorageService('audit_general', $auditGeneralEntityManager) ); CAUTION When more than one StorageService is registered, a storage_mapper must be provided. The provider throws a ProviderException if it cannot determine which storage service to use.

documents.t: The storage mapper can also be set after the provider is created: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService; $provider->getConfiguration()->setStorageMapper( function (string $entity, array $services): StorageService { return $services['audit_general']; } );

WARNING When using separate databases, the audit write and the application write happen in different database connections: the audit entries are written on the storage connection just before the application transaction is committed. When that transaction turns out to be rolled back (the audit fails, or the server reports a rollback when committing), the provider deletes the audit entries it has just written on the storage connection. This clean-up is best effort: when the outcome of the COMMIT is unknown (e.g. the connection is lost), the audit entries are kept: an orphan entry is better than a missing one; when the deletion itself fails, the entries are left behind and the failure is reported, without hiding the original error, to the PSR-3 logger of the provider, with the transaction_id of the entries and the audit table: $provider->setLogger($logger); // any Psr\Log\LoggerInterface For strict transactional consistency, keep auditing and storage on the same EntityManager/connection.

Cost of auditing a flush, and duration of the schema v2 migration This page gives measured figures for the flush pipeline of the provider (audit entries built in onFlush and written before the COMMIT), comparing the latest 1.x release with 2.0, with and without batch INSERT, and the duration of audit:schema:migrate on a large schema v1 table. They come from one machine: use them as orders of magnitude and to compare configurations, and measure your own workload before relying on a precise figure.

2.0 with batch_size: 0 (the default) costs about the same as 1.2.1: from 10 % faster to 2 % slower on SQLite, within ±3 % on PostgreSQL from 500 entities per flush. On MySQL, and with 50 entities per flush, the differences in either direction stay within the dispersion of the measurements. 2.0 with batch_size: 500 writes the audit entries of a flush with multi-row INSERT statements. With 500 or 1,000 entities per flush, a flush is 10 to 18 % faster than with 1.2.1 on SQLite, 19 to 51 % faster on MySQL and 44 to 67 % faster on PostgreSQL. The more round trips cost (a remote database server, a network), the larger the gain. Before the 2.0 release, fewer indexes, RETURNING id on PostgreSQL, a lighter transaction page, deferred joins for deep pages on MySQL and a batched audit:snapshot: see Before the 2.0 release. Migrating a 1,000,000-row schema v1 audit table with audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all took 5 minutes on MySQL and 3 minutes on PostgreSQL. See Schema v2 migration.

A last series of optimizations landed before the 2.0 release, each measured with the PHPBench suites of benchmarks/ (AuditBench, ReadBench, SnapshotBench), main before the changes against the branch, back to back on the same machine: Change Measured effect 3 secondary indexes fewer on audit tables (object_id, blame_id and discriminator alone) Flushes 20 to 28 % faster on PostgreSQL; indexes 30 % smaller on MySQL (raw INSERTs 18 % faster on a 300,000-row table) INSERT … RETURNING id on PostgreSQL with batch_size: 0 (no SELECT LASTVAL() per entry) Included in the PostgreSQL figures above (raw INSERT: 152-178 → 82-87 µs per row) Reader::getAuditsByTransactionId() introspects each audit table only, not the whole database Transaction page 89 to 99 % faster (200 unrelated tables) Deep pages of an unfiltered query read with a deferred join on MySQL and MariaDB Page 500 of 1,000: 55 → 4 ms on MySQL audit:snapshot writes multi-row INSERTs and loads the association targets of a batch together Snapshot 40 % faster on SQLite, 73 % on MySQL, 79 % on PostgreSQL extra_data_provider called once per flush; driver, storage mapper and association metadata resolved once Within the dispersion of the flush figures

The benchmark is benchmarks/AuditBench.php (PHPBench). Each scenario changes N entities of the test fixtures (Author, Post, Tag), all audited, and measures the single flush() that writes them — the Doctrine work and the auditing (changesets, diffs, audit rows). The schema is rebuilt and the data seeded before each iteration, outside the measured time. Scenario Measured flush Audit rows insert insert N authors N update update 3 fields of N posts N remove remove N authors N associate add a tag to N posts (many-to-many) 2N dissociate remove that tag from N posts 2N mixed insert N/2 authors, update N/4 of the existing ones (2 fields), remove N/4 N Three configurations were measured back to back, for each database and each N: Configuration Code 1.2.1 tag 1.2.1 (latest 1.x release), schema v1 2.0-dev, batch_size: 0 main at 169793e (batch INSERT), schema v2, one INSERT per entry¹ 2.0-dev, batch_size: 500 the same code with batch_size: 500 ¹ The PostgreSQL N = 50 triplet was run again on main at ae51e10, which only changes audit:schema:migrate (see Reading the results). That is 50 audit rows and 3 transactions per cycle, i.e. 60,000 transactions for 1,000,000 rows (547 MiB on MySQL, 447 MiB on PostgreSQL). Run: one database after the other, nothing else running; the command output is timestamped to get the duration of each step.

Step MySQL 8.0 PostgreSQL 15 Additive DDL (new columns, schema_version, blame) 50 s 43 s transaction_hash → transaction_id (60,000 ULIDs) 100 s 29 s Diffs conversion (1,000,000 rows) 139 s 118 s Legacy columns dropped < 1 s < 1 s Total 4 min 59 s 3 min 13 s Table size after OPTIMIZE TABLE / VACUUM FULL 690 MiB (+26 %) 614 MiB (+37 %) After the migration, both tables had 60,000 distinct transaction_id values (one per legacy transaction, the grouping is kept), no row without transaction_id, blame or source in its diffs, and every row at schema_version 2. What takes the time: every row is read, its diffs decoded, rewritten in the v2 envelope and updated. Both conversions work in batches of 500 rows (or transactions), each written in one database transaction, and read the rows through the primary key or the transaction_hash index: their duration grows linearly with the size of the audit tables. Your own estimate: --limit=N converts only N transactions or rows and keeps the legacy columns, so that a later run resumes where it stopped. Time a run on a sample and extrapolate linearly; test on a copy of your production data, with a backup, before the real migration.

Create and manage audit tables in your database This guide covers how to create and manage audit tables using the SchemaManager.

For each audited entity, the provider creates a corresponding audit table to store the change history. The SchemaManager class handles all schema operations using DBAL's schema introspection API. The schema can be managed in two ways: Automatically — via Doctrine's postGenerateSchemaTable event (integrates with doctrine:schema:update / Migrations) Manually — by calling SchemaManager::updateAuditSchema() directly

Each audit table created by the current provider has the following structure: CREATE TABLE posts_audit ( id BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, schema_version SMALLINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 2, type VARCHAR(11) NOT NULL, object_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, discriminator VARCHAR(255) NULL, transaction_id CHAR(26) NULL, diffs JSON NULL, extra_data JSON NULL, blame_id VARCHAR(255) NULL, blame JSON NULL, created_at DATETIME NOT NULL, INDEX type_idx (type), INDEX object_id_type_idx (object_id, type), INDEX transaction_id_idx (transaction_id), INDEX blame_id_created_at_idx (blame_id, created_at), INDEX created_at_idx (created_at) ); The SQL is illustrative: the actual index names are generated from a hash of the table name (type_<md5>_idx…), and the column types depend on the platform (JSON on MySQL / MariaDB, JSONB on PostgreSQL, TEXT on SQLite).

Column Type Description id BIGINT (PK) Auto-increment primary key schema_version SMALLINT Diffs format version: 1 (legacy) or 2 (current) type VARCHAR(11) Action: insert, update, remove, associate, dissociate object_id VARCHAR(255) The primary key of the audited entity discriminator VARCHAR(255) Entity class (used in inheritance hierarchies) transaction_id CHAR(26) ULID grouping changes from the same flush batch diffs JSON JSON-encoded change data (see format below) extra_data JSON Custom extra data (populated via LifecycleEvent listener) blame_id VARCHAR(255) User identifier who made the change blame JSON Blame: username, user_fqdn, user_firewall, ip, impersonator when the user is impersonated, and via when a blame context is set created_at DATETIME When the audit entry was created

All entry types share a unified JSON envelope: { "source": { "id": "42", "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Hello World", "table": "posts" }, "changes": { "title": { "old": "Hello World", "new": "Hello auditor!" }, "content": { "old": null, "new": "My first post." } } } source — always present: entity id, FQCN, label, and table at the time of the operation changes — field-level diff with explicit old/new for every operation: INSERT: old is always null UPDATE: both old and new reflect the changed values REMOVE: empty by default; with full_snapshot_on_remove, every audited field with its old value and a null new (a generated identifier, reset by Doctrine on deletion, is left out: the source block holds it), and every owning-side to-one association with the summary of its target as old snapshot — only on entries written by audit:snapshot: an insert entry with "snapshot": true records the state of an entity that existed before auditing started, not its creation (Entry::isSnapshot() reads it) ASSOCIATE / DISSOCIATE — use a different structure (no changes key): { "source": { "id": "1", "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Post #1", "table": "posts", "field": "tags" }, "target": { "id": "5", "class": "App\\Entity\\Tag", "label": "php", "table": "tag", "field": "posts" }, "is_owning_side": true, "join_table": "post__tag" }
Entries written by earlier versions of the provider carry schema_version = 1. The Entry model reads them transparently — see Entry Reference.

The provider writes audit rows on flush only. An application that writes rows itself (for example to import the history kept by another tool) must follow the format above, or the Reader and the viewer misread the rows without any error: Column What to write schema_version 2, always written explicitly: do not rely on the column default, which can still be 1 on a table left half-migrated or completed by hand; a row read as 1 has its diffs read as the legacy format type insert, update, remove, associate or dissociate object_id, discriminator the identifier of the entity as a string; its class in discriminator for an entity of an inheritance hierarchy, NULL otherwise transaction_id a ULID (26 characters, e.g. (string) new Ulid() with symfony/uid), the same for every row written by one flush (one transaction), across tables: the viewer and Query::transactions() group the entries by it diffs the envelope {"source": {…}, "changes": {"field": {"old": …, "new": …}}}, or the association structure; source holds id, class, label and table; plus deep_diffs (the fields whose change is a JSON deep diff) when relevant, without which the deep diffs are inferred from their shape blame_id, blame NULL and NULL when nobody is known; otherwise blame holds the four keys username, user_fqdn, user_firewall and ip, each set to null when unknown, plus impersonator and via when relevant extra_data a JSON object, or NULL created_at the date of the change, Y-m-d H:i:s, in the timezone of the configuration (timezone, UTC by default) diffs, blame and extra_data are JSONB on PostgreSQL: cast the values (::jsonb) in a hand-written INSERT. Rows written by hand go around the LifecycleEvent listeners of the application (extra data, rewriting of the diffs): apply their effect yourself. Rows of entities that declare an #[AuditRoot] are not indexed in audit_root: run audit:roots:rebuild after the import, or they are missing from the histories.

Creates audit tables for entities that don't have one yet, and adds missing columns to existing ones: // Create / update all audit tables $schemaManager->updateAuditSchema(); NOTE updateAuditSchema() is safe to run repeatedly. It checks for existing tables and columns before making changes.

Six console commands are available. audit:schema:update​ Creates new audit tables and updates existing ones to match the current schema. # Preview the SQL that would be executed php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql # Execute the changes php bin/console audit:schema:update --force # Both: show SQL and execute php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql --force audit:schema:migrate​ Migrates existing audit tables from schema version 1 to schema version 2. # Preview the SQL that would be executed (dry-run) php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --dump-sql --convert-all # Execute the migration and convert the existing rows (recommended) php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all # Convert a sample only, to estimate the duration (keeps the legacy columns, resumable) php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all --limit=10000 CAUTION The migration drops the legacy columns and cannot be undone: back up the audit tables first. transaction_hash is only dropped once converted (--convert-transaction-hash or --convert-all), or with --drop-transaction-hash, which drops it without converting it: legacy rows then lose their transaction grouping. Follow the upgrade guide for the complete procedure. NOTE Use audit:schema:migrate when upgrading an existing installation. New installations created with audit:schema:update already use schema version 2. NOTE --convert-diffs rewrites existing diffs rows in PHP (batches of 500). This can take a while on large tables. Without this flag, legacy rows remain readable via Entry::getDiffs() since the Entry model handles both schema versions transparently. audit:clean​ Removes audit entries older than a specified retention period (P12M by default). # Keep last 6 months (dry run) php bin/console audit:clean P6M --dry-run # Execute, skip confirmation (for cron jobs) php bin/console audit:clean P12M --no-confirm # Delete before a specific date php bin/console audit:clean --date=2024-01-01 --no-confirm # Exclude specific entities php bin/console audit:clean -x App\\Entity\\User # Include only specific entities php bin/console audit:clean -i App\\Entity\\Log Entities with a retention policy (#[Auditable(maxAge: …, maxEntries: …)], or the max_age / max_entries entity options) apply it: maxAge replaces the global cutoff, and maxEntries also deletes everything but the N most recent entries. See Retention Policy. audit:export​ Exports audit entries as NDJSON (default, recommended for large exports), JSON or CSV, streamed to the standard output or to a file. # Every auditable entity, NDJSON on stdout php bin/console audit:export # One entity, as CSV, for a period php bin/console audit:export App\\Entity\\Post --format=csv --from=2026-01-01 --to=2026-03-31 --output=posts.csv # One object, or one user, without the user and IP fields php bin/console audit:export App\\Entity\\Post --id=42 --anonymize php bin/console audit:export --blame-id=7 Each line or row is an Entry::toArray(): the same columns for legacy and schema v2 entries. audit:roots:rebuild​ Indexes the existing audit entries under their audit roots (#[AuditRoot], roots entity option), in the audit_root table: after declaring a new root, or after migrating audit tables to schema v2. php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild --entity='App\Entity\Comment' --dry-run Option Description --entity Entities whose entries are indexed (repeatable), all by default --dry-run Count the missing index rows, write nothing Only missing rows are written and no row is deleted, so the command can be run again and rows written by hand are kept. See Histories. audit:snapshot​ Records the current state of existing entities, so that their history does not start at their first change when auditing is enabled on a database that already holds data. Each entity gets one insert entry flagged with "snapshot": true, holding the current value of every audited field (old: null). # Snapshot some entities php bin/console audit:snapshot 'App\Entity\Post' 'App\Entity\Author' # Snapshot every audited entity, 1,000 rows per database transaction php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --batch-size=1000 # Count what would be written php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --dry-run Option Short Description --all -a Snapshot every audited entity (instead of the entities given as arguments) --batch-size -b Entities read and written per database transaction (default 500) --force -f Also snapshot entities that already have an audit history --dry-run Count the entities to snapshot, write nothing Idempotent: an entity that already has at least one audit entry is skipped, so the command can be run again (e.g. after an interruption). --force snapshots it anyway: a manual snapshot of its current state. Batches: entities are read in identifier order (keyset pagination), each batch is written in its own database transaction and its entries share one transaction_id. The entity manager is cleared between batches. Content: the same fields as an insert: ignored columns and generated identifiers are left out, owning-side to-one associations are summarized, JSON fields are deep diffs. To-many associations are not snapshotted. Context: created_at is the date of the snapshot, the blame is the console user (blame_id is null without a user provider). Doctrine filters that are enabled apply: rows they hide (e.g. soft-deleted) are not snapshotted. Inheritance: an entity whose parent class is also selected is read through its parent; each row is written to the audit table of its own class. The same logic is available in PHP through DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Snapshot\Snapshotter: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Snapshot\Snapshotter; $result = new Snapshotter($provider)->snapshot(Post::class, batchSize: 500); $result->read; // entities read $result->snapshotted; // entries written $result->skipped(); // entities that already had an audit history NOTE These commands use Symfony's Lock component to prevent concurrent execution. Registering Commands (Standalone)​ When not using auditor-bundle, register the commands manually: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\CleanAuditLogsCommand; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\ExportAuditLogsCommand; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\MigrateSchemaCommand; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\RebuildRootsCommand; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\SnapshotCommand; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\UpdateSchemaCommand; use Symfony\Component\Console\Application; $application = new Application(); foreach ([ new UpdateSchemaCommand(), new MigrateSchemaCommand(), new CleanAuditLogsCommand(), new SnapshotCommand(), new ExportAuditLogsCommand(), new RebuildRootsCommand(), ] as $command) { $application->addCommand($command->setAuditor($auditor)); } $application->run();

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Schema\SchemaManager; $schemaManager = new SchemaManager($provider); // Get SQL without executing $sqls = $schemaManager->getUpdateAuditSchemaSql(); // Execute all pending changes $schemaManager->updateAuditSchema(); // Execute with a progress callback $schemaManager->updateAuditSchema(null, function (array $progress) { echo sprintf('Progress: %d / %d', $progress['current'], $progress['total']); });
By default, audit tables are named: {entity_table}_audit Entity Table Audit Table users users_audit posts posts_audit blog_posts blog_posts_audit

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Configuration; // Prefix only: audit_posts $config = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => 'audit_', 'table_suffix' => '', ]); // Suffix only: posts_history $config = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => '', 'table_suffix' => '_history', ]); // Both: audit_posts_log $config = new Configuration([ 'table_prefix' => 'audit_', 'table_suffix' => '_log', ]);
When you add #[Auditable] to a new entity and add it to the configuration: Call $schemaManager->updateAuditSchema() to create the new audit table.
NOTE When you remove an entity from the auditing configuration, the audit table is not automatically deleted. Historical data is preserved. Drop the table manually if you no longer need it.

TIP Adding or removing fields from an entity requires no schema changes to the audit table. Diffs are stored as JSON, so new fields appear in future audits automatically and removed fields simply won't appear in new entries.

Native JSON column type is used for diffs, extra_data, and blame InnoDB engine is recommended for transactional integrity InnoDB does not compress anything by default. On MariaDB, enable the compression option to store diffs and extra_data as compressed columns (JSON COMPRESSED). MySQL has no column compression, so the compression option has no effect there. If disk space matters more than speed, InnoDB page compression can be enabled manually on audit tables (requires innodb_file_per_table and a file system supporting hole punching, e.g. ext4 or XFS): ALTER TABLE posts_audit COMPRESSION='zlib'; OPTIMIZE TABLE posts_audit; -- compresses existing rows Doctrine does not manage table compression options: this is neither reported nor reverted by schema commands.

Native JSONB column type is used for diffs, extra_data and blame Large JSONB values are compressed automatically (TOAST): the compression option is not needed and has no effect Audit tables created with JSON columns by previous versions are converted to JSONB by audit:schema:update (or by your next migration if you manage audit tables with Doctrine Migrations) Indexed columns use PostgreSQL-compatible index names
NOTE SQLite is recommended for development and testing only. It supports JSON operations natively from version 3.38+.

Few indexes — (object_id, type) and (blame_id, created_at) cover the most frequent Reader query patterns, and every other secondary index slows each audit INSERT down: there is none on object_id, blame_id or discriminator alone (5 secondary indexes instead of 8 before 2.0: audit INSERTs about 18 % faster on MySQL, indexes 30 % smaller) JSON storage — Native JSON types (MySQL, PostgreSQL) provide best query performance on diffs and blame Archiving — Implement a periodic cleanup strategy for high-volume applications using audit:clean Separate database — Consider storing audits in a dedicated database to avoid impacting application performance

AuditingService and StorageService — the building blocks of the DoctrineProvider The DoctrineProvider relies on two types of services: AuditingService (source of changes) and StorageService (destination of audit entries).

Service Interface Responsibility AuditingService AuditingServiceInterface Wraps an EntityManager and captures entity changes StorageService StorageServiceInterface Wraps an EntityManager used to persist audit entries Both services extend DoctrineService and wrap a Doctrine EntityManagerInterface.

The AuditingService wraps the EntityManager whose entities should be audited. When DoctrineProvider::registerAuditingService() is called, it registers the DoctrineSubscriber on the event manager of the entity manager. The AuditorMiddleware is not added for you: it must be in the middlewares of the DBAL connection (see below).

$provider->registerAuditingService($auditingService); // ↑ This attaches DoctrineSubscriber to the event manager of the entity manager (onFlush, postFlush). // The connection must have been created with the AuditorMiddleware. IMPORTANT The EntityManager must be configured before the provider is registered with the auditor. The AuditorMiddleware must be present in the DBAL middleware stack for the transactional flush callback to work: without it, nothing is audited. $dbalConfiguration = new \Doctrine\DBAL\Configuration(); $dbalConfiguration->setMiddlewares([new \DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\DBAL\Middleware\AuditorMiddleware()]); $connection = \Doctrine\DBAL\DriverManager::getConnection($connectionParams, $dbalConfiguration); auditor-bundle adds it to the connections of the auditing entity managers.

registerAuditingService() attaches the listeners when it runs, that is when the provider is built: a flush run before that is not audited. A dependency injection container can declare them instead, as lazy listeners of the event managers: they are registered with the event manager when it is created, and the provider is built on the first flush (auditor-bundle does it): $provider->disableListenerAttachment(); // before registerAuditingService() $provider->registerAuditingService(new AuditingService('default', $entityManager)); // then, on the event manager of each auditing entity manager: // - $provider->getDoctrineSubscriber() on onFlush, postFlush (and Gedmo's postSoftDelete) // - new CreateSchemaListener($provider) on postGenerateSchemaTable // (TableSchemaListener does nothing any more: it is not needed) The subscriber is shared by all the auditing entity managers, whose state it keeps apart: entity managers sharing an event manager (as on one DoctrineBundle connection) get it once. WARNING Before 6.4.44, 7.4.17 and 8.1.5, the ContainerAwareEventManager of Symfony's doctrine-bridge drops a listener attached while it initializes its lazy listeners of the same event: a lazy onFlush listener that only builds the provider would lose the subscriber. Declare the subscriber itself as the listener.
The StorageService wraps the EntityManager used to write audit rows. This can be the same EntityManager as the auditing service (single database) or a different one (multi-database).

The most common setup uses the same EntityManager for both services: <?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService; $provider->registerAuditingService(new AuditingService('default', $entityManager)); $provider->registerStorageService(new StorageService('default', $entityManager));

For multi-database setups, register multiple services with distinct names and configure a storage mapper: <?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService; // $appEntityManager reads/writes your application data // $auditEntityManager writes audit rows to a separate database $provider->registerAuditingService( new AuditingService('app', $appEntityManager) ); $provider->registerStorageService( new StorageService('audit', $auditEntityManager) ); NOTE See Multi-Database for a complete guide including the storage_mapper callback.

// Get all registered auditing services $auditingServices = $provider->getAuditingServices(); // Get all registered storage services $storageServices = $provider->getStorageServices(); // Get the underlying EntityManager from a service $em = $storageService->getEntityManager();

When running auditor inside Symfony Messenger workers, the EntityManager is reset between messages by Symfony's services_resetter. Without proper handling, only the first message is audited correctly — subsequent messages silently fail because: The DoctrineSubscriber would hold a stale EntityManager reference. The DoctrineProvider would reuse cached PreparedStatement objects bound to a closed connection. DoctrineProvider implements Symfony\Contracts\Service\ResetInterface. Its reset() method clears the prepared statement cache and resets all subscriber transaction caches, ensuring clean state between messages.

For Symfony to call reset() automatically between messages, tag DoctrineProvider with kernel.reset: With autoconfigure: true (recommended) If your service definition uses autoconfigure: true, Symfony detects ResetInterface and registers the tag automatically — no additional config needed. Manual tag # config/services.yaml services: DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\DoctrineProvider: tags: - { name: kernel.reset, method: reset } NOTE If you use damienharper/auditor-bundle, check the bundle's documentation for its service configuration — the tag may already be applied.

Read and query audit entries with the Reader and Query APIs This guide covers how to read and query audit entries using the Reader and Query APIs.

The DoctrineProvider includes a querying system built on top of Doctrine DBAL: Reader — Factory for creating queries and utilities Query — Builds and executes audit queries against DBAL Filters — Filter results by various criteria Entry — Represents a single audit log entry

// Simple query for all audits of an entity $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class); $audits = $query->execute(); // Query with options $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, [ 'object_id' => 42, // Specific entity ID 'type' => 'update', // Action type 'page' => 1, // Pagination 'page_size' => 20, ]);

Option Type Default Description object_id int|string|array null Filter by entity ID(s) type string|array null Filter by action type(s) blame_id int|string|array null Filter by user ID(s) who made changes user_id int|string|array null Alias for blame_id transaction_id string|array null Filter by transaction ID(s) (ULID) changed_field string|list<string> null Entries whose diff touches this field, or one of these fields (see ChangedFieldFilter) blame_origin string|BlameOrigin|array null Entries made from these origins (see BlameOriginFilter) page int|null 1 Page number (1-based) page_size int|null 50 Number of entries per page strict bool true With single table inheritance, keep only the entries of the queried class (filter on the discriminator)
// Returns an array of Entry objects $entries = $query->execute(); // Returns the total count (ignoring pagination) $total = $query->count();

<?php $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class); $result = $reader->paginate($query, page: 2, pageSize: 25); // $result contains: // 'results' → \ArrayIterator<int|string, Entry> // 'currentPage' → int // 'hasPreviousPage' → bool // 'hasNextPage' → bool // 'previousPage' → int|null // 'nextPage' → int|null // 'numPages' → int // 'haveToPaginate' → bool // 'numResults' → int // 'pageSize' → int foreach ($result['results'] as $entry) { echo $entry->type . ': ' . $entry->objectId . "\n"; }

A transaction (an action: the flushes of one database transaction share its id) often writes several entries, so pages of entries cut actions and hold a varying number of them. transactions() pages the transactions the query reads instead, with its filters (its order and limit do not apply), most recent first: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\SimpleFilter; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, ['page_size' => null]); $total = $query->countTransactions(); $transactions = $query->transactions(limit: 25, offset: 25); // list<TransactionSummary>, page 2 // then the entries of these transactions, with the same filters, most recent first $ids = array_values(array_filter(array_map(static fn ($transaction) => $transaction->transactionId, $transactions))); $entries = $query->transactionEntries($ids); // or transactionEntries($ids, limit: 1000) // an entry without transaction id is a transaction of its own foreach ($transactions as $transaction) { if (null === $transaction->transactionId && $transaction->table === $query->getTable()) { $entries = [...$entries, ...(clone $query)->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::ID, (string) $transaction->entryId))->execute()]; } } A TransactionSummary tells its transactionId, the date of its most recent entry (createdAt) and its number of entries. Transactions are ordered by that date, then by transaction id (both descending). An entry written without transaction id is a transaction of its own: transactionId is null, entryId and table identify it. A table not migrated to schema v2 is read through its transaction_hash column; in a table being migrated (audit:schema:migrate without --convert-transaction-hash), a row not converted yet stands for its transaction by its hash, as $entry->transactionId does, and transactionEntries() reads it too. Query::transactionsOf($queries, $limit, $offset) and Query::countTransactionsOf($queries) do the same across several audit tables (one query per table): a transaction that wrote in several tables is one transaction. The tables of one connection are read in one statement; across connections, each one is read for $offset + $limit transactions. A transaction stored on two connections is listed once but counted twice (the last page may come out short), and its number of entries only counts the part read on each connection. When the transactions are read on one audit table (a query alone, or the only table of its connection), a page that ends within the first 10,000 transactions walks the entries most recent first, on the created_at index, until it has found them. Measured with 3,000,000 entries in 750,000 transactions, by pages of 50: page 1 in 2 to 6 ms, page 100 in 40 to 100 ms, instead of 1.3 to 25 s. A deep page with a very selective filter that the date order does not serve (one user, anonymous entries) can be slower than grouping: up to 1.4 s instead of 75 ms on PostgreSQL. The other pages group the entries the filters keep, in the database: deeper pages; a page whose walk reads, or would read, more than 50,000 entries (very large transactions); a table being migrated; several tables of one connection, read in one statement. On a large table without a selective filter, such a page costs a pass over the table, and so does countTransactions(). countTransactionsByDay() counts the transactions the query reads by day of their entries, for an activity graph: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\DateRangeFilter; $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, ['page_size' => null]) ->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(Query::CREATED_AT, new DateTimeImmutable('-29 days midnight'))); $query->countTransactionsByDay(); // ['2026-11-24' => 13, '2026-11-25' => 4] Days are those of the created_at column as stored (DATE(created_at)), in ascending order; days without any transaction are left out. A transaction whose entries span midnight counts on each of its days, as a filter on either day finds it.

Retrieve all audit entries related to the same database transaction across all configured entities: <?php // Get all entries that belong to the same transaction $byEntity = $reader->getAuditsByTransactionId('01JH8Z6Q3C2V5W7X9Y0A1B2C3D'); // Returns: ['App\Entity\Post' => [Entry, ...], 'App\Entity\Comment' => [Entry, ...]] foreach ($byEntity as $entityClass => $entries) { echo "Entity: $entityClass\n"; foreach ($entries as $entry) { echo ' ' . $entry->type . ' #' . $entry->objectId . "\n"; } } NOTE getAuditsByTransactionId() silently skips entities for which the current user does not have the view role. getAuditsByTransactionHash() is deprecated: it forwards to getAuditsByTransactionId(), which also finds the rows of tables not migrated yet by their legacy transaction_hash.

For advanced filtering not covered by the createQuery options, add filters directly on the Query object: <?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\DateRangeFilter; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; $query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class); // Filter by date range $query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter( Query::CREATED_AT, new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-01'), new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-12-31') )); $entries = $query->execute(); See Filters Reference for all available filters.

Entry objects use virtual properties (not getter methods): foreach ($entries as $entry) { $entry->id; // int - audit entry ID $entry->type; // string - 'insert', 'update', 'remove', 'associate', 'dissociate' $entry->objectId; // string - entity primary key $entry->transactionId; // string|null - ULID $entry->extraData; // array|null - already decoded from JSON $entry->userId; // int|string|null - blame_id $entry->username; // string|null - from blame JSON $entry->userFqdn; // string|null - from blame JSON $entry->userFirewall; // string|null - from blame JSON $entry->ip; // string|null - from blame JSON $entry->createdAt; // \DateTimeImmutable } IMPORTANT $entry->extraData is already decoded: it returns ?array, not a JSON string. Do not call json_decode() on it. Read the diffs with $entry->getDiffs(). See Entry Reference for a complete description.

Reader::createQuery() automatically checks the role checker before returning the query: use DH\Auditor\Exception\AccessDeniedException; try { $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Payment::class); } catch (AccessDeniedException $e) { // Current user does not have permission to view Payment audits }

The audit log entry model An Entry object represents a single audit log record. It is returned by Query::execute() and is part of the damienharper/auditor core library.
use DH\Auditor\Model\Entry; Entry is a read-only value object hydrated from a database row.

Entry exposes its data through virtual properties (not getter methods). Access them directly: Property Type Description $id int Auto-increment primary key of the audit entry $schemaVersion int Diffs format version: 1 (legacy) or 2 (current). Defaults to 1. $type string Action type: insert, update, remove, associate, dissociate $objectId string Primary key of the audited entity $discriminator string|null Entity class (used in inheritance hierarchies) $transactionId string|null ULID grouping changes from the same flush batch $extraData array|null Already-decoded extra data (do not call json_decode()) $userId int|string|null Identifier of the user who made the change (blame_id) $blame array|null Decoded blame context: username, user_fqdn, user_firewall, ip, plus impersonator and via when set $username string|null Convenience shortcut for $blame['username'] $userFqdn string|null Convenience shortcut for $blame['user_fqdn'] $userFirewall string|null Convenience shortcut for $blame['user_firewall'] $ip string|null Convenience shortcut for $blame['ip'] $impersonator array|null User who impersonated the blamed one (id, username, fqdn), from $blame['impersonator'] $via array|null Blame context (type, label, data) the change was made in, from $blame['via'] $createdAt \DateTimeImmutable Timestamp of when the audit entry was created $entity string|null FQCN of the audited entity, set by readers that merge several audit tables (history of a root) $rootPath string|null Path that led to the root in the history of a root (null for the root itself) isDeepDiff($field) tells whether a field's changeset is a JSON deep diff, and getSortKey() gives a total order of entries across tables (see Histories). IMPORTANT $entry->type is a plain string (e.g. 'insert', 'update'), not an enum. $entry->extraData is already decoded — it returns ?array. Never call json_decode() on it.

Use getDiffs() to access the field-level change data: $audits = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['object_id' => 42])->execute(); foreach ($audits as $entry) { // getDiffs() returns the 'changes' sub-array for schema v2 entries // and the raw diff array for legacy schema v1 entries foreach ($entry->getDiffs() as $field => $change) { $old = $change['old'] ?? '(null)'; $new = $change['new'] ?? '(null)'; echo " $field: $old → $new\n"; } }

All entry types use the same unified envelope. getDiffs() returns the changes sub-array directly. insert — old is always null: { "title": { "old": null, "new": "Hello World" }, "content": { "old": null, "new": "My first post." } } update: { "title": { "old": "Hello World", "new": "Hello auditor!" } } remove — empty by default (the source block identifies the deleted entity); with the full_snapshot_on_remove option, every audited field and owning-side to-one association, new always null (except a generated identifier, which only the source block holds): { "title": { "old": "Hello auditor!", "new": null }, "content": { "old": "My first post.", "new": null }, "author": { "old": { "id": 1, "class": "App\\Entity\\Author", "label": "John", "table": "author" }, "new": null } } associate / dissociate — no changes key; getDiffs() returns the full envelope: { "source": { "id": "1", "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Post #1", "table": "posts", "field": "tags" }, "target": { "id": "5", "class": "App\\Entity\\Tag", "label": "php", "table": "tag", "field": "posts" }, "is_owning_side": true, "join_table": "post__tag" }

For schema v2 entries, use getDiffSource() and getDiffTarget(): // getDiffSource(): entity metadata at the time of the operation (all types) $source = $entry->getDiffSource(); // ['class' => 'App\Entity\Post', 'id' => '42', 'label' => 'Hello World', 'table' => 'posts'] // getDiffTarget(): second entity in associate/dissociate entries $target = $entry->getDiffTarget(); // ['class' => 'App\Entity\Tag', 'field' => 'posts', 'id' => '5', 'label' => 'php', 'table' => 'tag'] Both return null for legacy schema v1 entries.

audit:snapshot records the state of entities that existed before auditing started as insert entries flagged with "snapshot": true. isSnapshot() tells them from real insertions (always false on schema v1): if ('insert' === $entry->type && $entry->isSnapshot()) { // state of the entity at $entry->createdAt, when it was snapshotted: not its creation }

getDiffs() returns the raw decoded array as-is, minus the internal @source key that legacy inserts carry (getDiffSource() returns null for legacy entries): insert (as returned by getDiffs()): { "title": { "new": "Hello World" }, "content": { "new": "My first post." } } update: { "title": { "old": "Hello World", "new": "Hello auditor!" } } remove: { "id": 42, "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Hello auditor!", "table": "posts" }
// $entry->extraData is already decoded — no json_decode() needed if (null !== $entry->extraData) { echo 'Reason: ' . ($entry->extraData['reason'] ?? 'unknown') . "\n"; }

The $createdAt property is a \DateTimeImmutable object. Its timezone is set to the timezone configured in the auditor Configuration: $configuration = new Configuration(['timezone' => 'Europe/Paris']); // ... foreach ($entries as $entry) { $dt = $entry->createdAt; echo $dt->format('Y-m-d H:i:s T'); // e.g., 2024-06-15 14:30:00 CEST }

<?php use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Reader; $reader = new Reader($provider); $entries = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, [ 'object_id' => 42, 'page' => 1, 'page_size' => 10, ])->execute(); foreach ($entries as $entry) { $source = $entry->getDiffSource(); printf( "[%s] %s #%s — by %s (%s) from %s at %s\n", $entry->type, $source['class'] ?? App\Entity\Post::class, $entry->objectId, $entry->username ?? 'anonymous', $entry->userId ?? '-', $entry->ip ?? '-', $entry->createdAt->format('Y-m-d H:i:s') ); foreach ($entry->getDiffs() as $field => $change) { if (!\is_array($change) || $entry->isDeepDiff($field)) { continue; // association entries and JSON deep diffs have another shape } printf(" %s: %s → %s\n", $field, json_encode($change['old'] ?? null), json_encode($change['new'] ?? null)); } }
