Fine-grained control over audit queries Filters allow you to restrict the results returned by a Query. They can be added via createQuery() options or directly on the Query object.

Filter Class Description SimpleFilter SimpleFilter Equality or IN match on a column DateRangeFilter DateRangeFilter Filter by a date range on a datetime column RangeFilter RangeFilter Filter by a numeric range NullFilter NullFilter Filter for NULL / NOT NULL values JsonFilter JsonFilter Filter by a value inside a JSON column, typically extra_data ChangedFieldFilter ChangedFieldFilter Entries whose diff touches a given field (or one of several) BlameOriginFilter BlameOriginFilter Entries made from some origins: web request, console, worker, system ImpersonatorFilter ImpersonatorFilter Entries made while a user impersonated another one, optionally by a given impersonator RootFilter RootFilter Entries indexed under an audit root (see Histories) All filter classes live under: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\{FilterClass}; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;
Matches a single value or a list of values (generates = ? or IN (?,?) SQL).

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\SimpleFilter; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; // Match a single value $query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::TYPE, 'update')); // Match multiple values (IN clause) $query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::TYPE, ['insert', 'update'])); // Filter by user ID $query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::USER_ID, 'user-42')); // Filter by entity ID $query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::OBJECT_ID, '100'));

Constant Column Query::ID id Query::TYPE type Query::OBJECT_ID object_id Query::DISCRIMINATOR discriminator Query::TRANSACTION_ID transaction_id Query::USER_ID blame_id NOTE Query::TRANSACTION_HASH is kept for backward compatibility and maps to transaction_id (same as Query::TRANSACTION_ID). Use Query::TRANSACTION_ID in new code.
Filters entries by a date range on created_at.

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\DateRangeFilter; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; // Entries created in January 2024 $query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter( Query::CREATED_AT, new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-01'), new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-31') )); // Entries created after a given date (open end) $query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter( Query::CREATED_AT, new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-06-01'), null )); // Entries created before a given date (open start) $query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter( Query::CREATED_AT, null, new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-06-01') ));
Filters entries by a numeric range (e.g., id between two values).

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\RangeFilter; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; // Entries with ID between 100 and 200 $query->addFilter(new RangeFilter(Query::ID, 100, 200)); // IDs greater than 500 (open end) $query->addFilter(new RangeFilter(Query::ID, 500, null));
Filters entries where a column is NULL or NOT NULL.

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\NullFilter; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; // Entries where blame_id IS NULL (anonymous changes) $query->addFilter(new NullFilter(Query::USER_ID)); NullFilter only tests IS NULL. To keep the entries whose column is not null, use a RangeFilter or a SimpleFilter with the values you expect, or a JsonFilter with IS NOT NULL on a JSON column. WARNING NullFilter works on indexed columns such as blame_id, object_id, type, etc. Do not use Query::JSON with NullFilter — there is no json column in the audit table. To find entries where extra_data IS NULL, query without a filter and check $entry->extraData === null.
Filters entries on a value inside a JSON column, typically extra_data: new JsonFilter($column, $path, $value = null, $operator = '=', $strict = false).

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\JsonFilter; // Entries whose extra_data.department is 'IT' $query->addFilter(new JsonFilter('extra_data', 'department', 'IT')); // Entries whose extra_data has a non-null 'route' $query->addFilter(new JsonFilter('extra_data', 'route', null, 'IS NOT NULL')); Operators: =, !=, <>, LIKE, NOT LIKE, IN, NOT IN, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL. On a platform without JSON support, the filter falls back to LIKE unless $strict is true (it then throws). See Extra Data for the platforms and indexing. TIP To find the entries that changed a field, use ChangedFieldFilter rather than a JsonFilter on diffs.

Restricts the results to the entries whose diff touches a given field, whatever the operation: inserts and updates that changed the field; removes recorded with full_snapshot_on_remove enabled (removes without a snapshot carry no field); associations and dissociations recorded on the field, so that filtering on a collection returns the items added to or removed from it. Both diff formats are read: the schema v2 envelope (including the rows converted by audit:schema:migrate --convert-diffs) and the legacy rows (schema_version = 1) that were not converted yet.

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\ChangedFieldFilter; // Through the createQuery() option $query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['changed_field' => 'title']); // Or directly on the query $query->addFilter(new ChangedFieldFilter('tags')); // Fields of embeddables use their dotted name $query->addFilter(new ChangedFieldFilter('address.street')); // Entries that changed any of several fields $query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['changed_field' => ['title', 'body']]); The field name must be a Doctrine field name (letters, digits and underscores, dotted for embeddables), otherwise an InvalidArgumentException is thrown. It is always passed to the database as a bound parameter. NOTE ChangedFieldFilter requires native JSON support (MySQL 5.7+, MariaDB 10.2.3+, PostgreSQL 9.4+, SQLite 3.38+) and an audit table with the schema v2 structure: run audit:schema:migrate on legacy tables first. It throws an InvalidArgumentException otherwise; check JsonPlatformHelper::isJsonSearchSupported() beforehand to offer the filter only where it works. TIP The predicate cannot use an index: the database reads the diffs of every row left by the other filters. Combine it with object_id or a date range on large audit tables.

Keeps the entries made from some origins (DH\Auditor\History\BlameOrigin): http (a web request with a firewall), console, messenger (blame context types) or system (anything else). Several origins are combined with OR. It reads the blame JSON column, so it needs native JSON support and a schema v2 table. use DH\Auditor\History\BlameOrigin; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\BlameOriginFilter; $query->addFilter(new BlameOriginFilter([BlameOrigin::Console, BlameOrigin::Messenger])); // Or through the createQuery() option $query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['blame_origin' => 'http']);

Keeps the entries made while a user impersonated another one (switch user): those whose blame JSON has an impersonator key, written when the user provider returns a user with an impersonator. Given an identifier, it keeps those of that impersonator only. It reads the blame JSON column, so it needs native JSON support and a schema v2 table. use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\ImpersonatorFilter; $query->addFilter(new ImpersonatorFilter()); // made by impersonating someone $query->addFilter(new ImpersonatorFilter('1')); // made by impersonator #1 Entries written before the impersonator key existed are not found: auditor-bundle before 8.0 appended the impersonator to the username instead (alice[impersonator admin]).

Keeps the entries indexed under an audit root, optionally through some paths only. It reads the audit_root index table: use it through Reader::createRootQuery(), which sets the index table and merges the tables of every entity (see Histories).

Multiple filters are combined with AND: use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\{DateRangeFilter, SimpleFilter}; use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query; $query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class); // All updates by user '42' in the last 30 days $query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::TYPE, 'update')); $query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::USER_ID, '42')); $query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter( Query::CREATED_AT, new \DateTimeImmutable('-30 days'), null )); $entries = $query->execute();
// Default order: created_at DESC, id DESC // Override: $query->addOrderBy(Query::CREATED_AT, 'ASC'); $query->addOrderBy(Query::ID, 'ASC');
// 20 results starting at offset 40 (page 3 of 20 per page) $query->limit(20, 40); $entries = $query->execute();

Read the history of a business object across several audit tables, and the last change of each field The building blocks (#[AuditRoot], HistoryGrouper, ChangeExtractor, BlameOrigin) are described in the auditor documentation. This page covers what the Doctrine provider adds: the audit root index, the history of a root, and field-level queries.

With the #[AuditRoot] attribute, or the roots entity option (both are merged): use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable; use DH\Auditor\Attribute\AuditRoot; #[ORM\Entity] #[Auditable] #[AuditRoot('property')] #[AuditRoot('visit.property')] class VisitReport { /* … */ } $configuration = new Configuration([ 'entities' => [ App\Entity\VisitReport::class => ['roots' => ['property', 'visit.property']], ], ]); A path is a list of single-valued association properties (ManyToOne, OneToOne, owning or inverse side) separated by dots. A collection in a path is an error, raised at the first flush of the entity. Roots declared on a parent class are inherited. For roots that a path cannot express (a polymorphic owner stored as a class and an id, a root picked by business rules), give the provider a root_resolver: a callable that receives an audited entity and returns its extra roots, keyed by a name of your choice, written as the root path of the index rows (null roots are skipped): $configuration->setRootResolver(static fn (object $entity): array => match (true) { $entity instanceof Attachment => ['subject' => $entity->getSubject()], default => [], });

When at least one entity has roots, audit:schema:update creates one more table per storage, audit_root (with the table_prefix), which indexes each audit entry under its roots: Column Content root_class FQCN of the root, the root class of its inheritance hierarchy root_id identifier of the root root_path path (or resolver key) that led to the root audit_table, object_id, transaction_id the audit entry created_at date of the audit entry Rows are written in the same database transaction as the audit entries (batched with them when batch_size is set). The roots are resolved during the flush: when the first association of a path changes, the entry is indexed under the old and the new root: moving a visit report to another property shows in both histories; the owner of an inverse OneToOne not set in memory is looked up among the entities being inserted or updated; removed entities are indexed while they still know their roots, so their history stays in the history of the root.

php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild # every entity with roots php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild --entity='App\Entity\VisitReport' --dry-run The command replays the diffs of the existing schema v2 entries: the first segment of a path is read from the diffs of the entry's entity, the next ones from the audit history of the entities the path goes through, as they were when the entry was written. It writes the missing rows of the paths declared with #[AuditRoot] or roots, and never deletes a row: it can be run again safely, and rows you write yourself (for entries whose diffs do not hold the association, such as imported or legacy entries) are kept. Roots returned by a root_resolver cannot be replayed. Run it after declaring a new root, or after migrating audit tables to schema v2 (audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all): entries in schema v1 or without a transaction id are skipped and counted. The command fails when an --entity is not audited, when it already runs, or when the diffs of an entry cannot be read; in the last case the rows of the other entries are still written. Rows that no longer match the configuration (a removed path) are not cleaned up: delete them with SQL if needed. Index rows go with their entries: the retention pruning (audit:clean and the scheduled retention) deletes the rows whose entry it deleted, and a rolled-back transaction deletes its rows from a remote storage along with its entries.

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Reader; $reader = new Reader($provider); $query = $reader->createRootQuery(Property::class, 42); $page = $query->fetch(20); // RootPage foreach ($page->group() as $item) { // list<HistoryItem>, one per transaction // $item->username, $item->origin, $item->getChanges()… } $next = $query->fetch(20, after: $page->lastCursor); $newer = $query->fetch(20, since: $page->firstCursor); // entries written since the page was read The query reads the entries of the root itself and those indexed under it, in every audit table concerned, and merges them: most recent first, then by transaction id, entity and id. Each Entry has $entry->entity (FQCN) and $entry->rootPath (null for the root itself). Pagination uses opaque cursors (keyset pagination), so a page never shifts when entries are written in the meantime. fetch() extends a page past its size until the transaction of its last entry is complete, so that an action is never split between two pages: pass the HistoryGrouper (or key callable) you display the page with to keep its groups whole, or false to cut the page at its size exactly. iterate() yields every entry, keyed by cursor, reading each table by batches; count() counts them. fetchTransactions() counts a page in transactions instead: every page but the last holds exactly that many actions, each one whole, whatever its number of entries. countTransactions() counts the transactions of the history, once each even when they wrote in several audit tables (twice when these tables are on two connections). $page = $query->fetchTransactions(20); // 20 actions $next = $query->fetchTransactions(20, after: $page->lastCursor); $total = $query->countTransactions(); A cursor that is not one (edited by hand in a query string, for instance) makes fetch() and iterate() throw an InvalidArgumentException. RootQuery::isCursor($cursor) tells it beforehand, to show the first page instead: $after = $request->query->getString('after'); $page = $query->fetch(20, after: RootQuery::isCursor($after) ? $after : null);

Option Type Default Description include ?list<string> null FQCNs of the entities to read (all by default) paths list<string> [] Root paths to keep (all by default). Leaves the entries of the root itself out self bool true Read the entries of the root itself type string|array null Operation types (insert, update…) blame_id int|string|array null Authors changed_field string|list<string> null Entries that changed one of the fields (native JSON needed) blame_origin string|BlameOrigin|array null http, console, messenger, system (native JSON needed) An entity in include that is not audited, or a path in paths that no entity declares (when no root_resolver is set), throws an InvalidArgumentException, as does a root class that no auditing entity manager maps. Only the view role of the root is checked: reading the history of a root gives access to the entries of the entities indexed under it. Use the read_scope option to restrict them further.

// last change of each field, or the creation (or snapshot) for a field never changed since $changes = $reader->getLastChanges(Property::class, 42, ['price', 'status']); $changes['price']?->getValue('price'); // value of the field: after the change, or at the creation (deep diff tree for a JSON field) $changes['price']?->getLabel('price'); // its label (#[DiffLabel], association), if any $changes['price']?->entry->username; // who, when: the Entry of the change $changes['price']?->entry->createdAt; // entries that changed a field, of one object or of all objects of a class $entries = $reader->getFieldHistory(Property::class, 42, 'price')->execute(); $entries = $reader->getFieldHistory(Property::class, null, 'price')->execute(); getLastChanges() returns array<string, ?Change> (null when nothing was audited). For a field never changed, the change is the creation of the object, which holds the requested fields: read the value with getValue($field) rather than new. For a JSON field changed since, getValue() returns the deep diff tree of the last change, not the whole value (ChangeKind::Json). It reads the entries that changed one of the fields when the platform has native JSON support, and scans the history of the object otherwise. getFieldHistory() returns a Query with a ChangedFieldFilter, which needs native JSON support. The changed_field option of createQuery() also takes a list of fields (entries that changed any of them), and blame_origin keeps the entries of some origins (BlameOriginFilter).

read_scope is a callable applied to every query the reader creates, including each table of a root query. It receives the query and the FQCN of the entity it reads, and can add filters, for instance to keep the entries of the current tenant (a RootFilter built by hand takes the root class of the inheritance hierarchy): $configuration->setReadScope(static function (Query $query, string $entity) use ($tenant): void { $query->addFilter(new JsonFilter('extra_data', 'tenant', $tenant->getId())); });

entity_label_resolver is a callable (see EntityLabelResolverInterface) that builds the label of an entity written in the source and target blocks of the diffs, and in association values. Return null to keep the default label (the string representation of the entity, otherwise Class#id); a Stringable is accepted. It runs during the flush and must not flush: an exception it throws aborts the flush and rolls the transaction back.

Migrate from auditor-doctrine-provider 1.x to 2.0 This guide covers upgrading from auditor-doctrine-provider 1.x to 2.0.

auditor-doctrine-provider 2.0 introduces schema version 2: a revised audit table format with a unified blame JSON column, a ULID-based transaction_id, and a richer diffs envelope. audit:schema:migrate converts the existing audit entries to the new format: the legacy columns are read during the migration, then dropped. There is no command to go back to the v1 schema: back up your audit tables before migrating (see below).

Scenario Impact Using damienharper/auditor-bundle 8.x ✅ Bundle handles wiring automatically Using auditor-doctrine-provider standalone ⚠️ Must migrate audit tables manually Custom providers calling persist(LifecycleEvent $event) ⚠️ Payload keys have changed Code reading $entry->transactionHash ⚠️ Property removed — use $entry->transactionId Code importing DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Attribute\{Auditable,Ignore,Security} ⚠️ Aliases removed — import DH\Auditor\Attribute\* Custom Doctrine types implementing NeedsConversionToAuditableType ⚠️ Implement DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Transaction\NeedsConversionToAuditableType LifecycleEvent listeners rewriting diffs ⚠️ Write under changes — see Listeners that rewrite diffs Audit tables created by Doctrine migrations ⚠️ A replayable migration is needed — see Audit tables managed by Doctrine Migrations Raw SQL on the audit tables ⚠️ Columns and diffs paths changed — see step 10 Code writing audit rows itself (imports) ⚠️ See Writing audit rows yourself

Migrating to 2.0 converts every existing audit table: plan it like a database migration, with a backup, a rehearsal on a copy of your data and a maintenance window. The steps below are in the order to follow.

Requirement 2.0 PHP 8.4 or later Symfony components 8.1 or later doctrine/dbal 4.6 or later doctrine/orm 3.7 or later damienharper/auditor 5.0 (requires symfony/uid, installed with it) damienharper/auditor-bundle (Symfony apps) 8.0 This guide starts from the latest 1.x release. From an older version, upgrade to the latest 1.x first and run audit:schema:update --force there, so that the audit tables match the last v1 schema before you migrate.

CAUTION There is no rollback. Once the conversions are done, audit:schema:migrate drops the legacy columns (transaction_hash, blame_user, blame_user_fqdn, blame_user_firewall, ip) and the indexes that cover them. A backup taken just before the migration is the only way back to 1.x and to the v1 data. Back up every audit table (*_audit by default, or your table_prefix / table_suffix), on every connection that stores audits when you use a storage_mapper. For example: # MySQL / MariaDB mysqldump --single-transaction my_database post_audit comment_audit > audit-backup.sql # PostgreSQL pg_dump --table='*_audit' my_database > audit-backup.sql

Restore a recent copy of your production database on a staging environment, install 2.0 there (step 5) and run the whole procedure. It tells you how long your maintenance window must be, and that the migration goes through on your data. The migration rewrites every audit row, so its duration grows linearly with the size of the audit tables. As an order of magnitude, count 3 to 5 minutes per million audit rows (a 1,000,000-row table took 4 min 59 s on MySQL 8.0 and 3 min 13 s on PostgreSQL 15 on a developer laptop, see Performance), plus the time audit:schema:update takes to apply the rest of the schema (step 7). To measure it on your own data without running the whole migration, convert a sample with --limit, on the copy: bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all --limit=10000 --limit=N (with a conversion option, not with --drop-transaction-hash) converts N transactions (--convert-transaction-hash) or N rows (--convert-diffs), prints an estimate of the remaining time, and keeps the legacy columns, so that a later run resumes where it stopped. WARNING Do not run --limit on production while 1.x still writes to it: it already adds the v2 columns and converts rows. Rehearse and estimate on a copy. Also check the free disk space: rows are rewritten in place, so the audit tables grow during the migration, up to 4 times their initial size on PostgreSQL in the measurement above, until the space is reused or reclaimed.

documents.t: 1.x writes v1 rows and 2.0 writes v2 rows: neither can write into a table that is half-way between the two. With 2.0, an audit entry that cannot be written makes the flush fail and the transaction roll back. So, for the duration of the migration, stop everything that modifies audited entities: put the application in maintenance mode, and stop the Messenger workers, cron jobs and scheduled tasks (including audit retention or audit:clean). Reading the audits is safe at any time: the Reader handles migrated and non-migrated tables. Histories across tables only index converted entries: run audit:roots:rebuild once the migration is complete (it warns about the entries it had to skip).
documents.s: 4️⃣ Stop writing audits during the migration

documents.t: # Symfony application composer require damienharper/auditor-bundle:^8.0 # This pulls in damienharper/auditor ^5.0 and damienharper/auditor-doctrine-provider ^2.0. # Without the bundle composer require damienharper/auditor:^5.0 damienharper/auditor-doctrine-provider:^2.0 Then clear the cache (bin/console cache:clear) and deploy the code, keeping the application in maintenance mode. CAUTION Do not let Doctrine change the audit tables before the migration. The provider declares the v2 audit tables in the Doctrine schema, so on v1 tables doctrine:schema:update --force and a migration generated by doctrine:migrations:diff drop the legacy columns without converting their data. Run audit:schema:migrate first; if your deployment runs doctrine:migrations:migrate automatically, make sure no pending migration touches the audit tables, and generate new migrations only after step 7. audit:schema:update refuses to run while an audit table still has the v1 schema. If your audit tables are created by Doctrine migrations, follow Audit tables managed by Doctrine Migrations instead: it replaces this advice. Audit tables managed by Doctrine Migrations​ When your audit tables are created by Doctrine migrations (generated by doctrine:migrations:diff, since the provider declares them in the Doctrine schema), audit:schema:migrate is not enough: it only migrates the databases it runs on: every database built by running the migrations from scratch (test databases, CI, new environments) still ends with v1 audit tables until a migration brings them to v2; the migration that doctrine:migrations:diff generates for that drops the legacy columns without converting their data, so it must not run on a database that holds audit entries; a deployment that runs doctrine:migrations:migrate when it starts runs it before you can run audit:schema:migrate. Write instead one migration whose every statement can be replayed: it brings an empty v1 table to v2, completes a table already migrated by audit:schema:migrate as audit:schema:update would, and changes nothing on a table already at v2. It stops while a table still has transaction_hash and rows, whose data only audit:schema:migrate can convert. Example for PostgreSQL, with the default index names (<columns>_<md5 of the audit table name, as written in TABLES>_idx): namespace DoctrineMigrations; use Doctrine\DBAL\Schema\Schema; use Doctrine\Migrations\AbstractMigration; final class Version20261201000000 extends AbstractMigration { // Every audit table, with your table_prefix / table_suffix. Unqualified names of tables in the current schema // (the first of search_path) only: the v1 check below does not see the other schemas. private const array TABLES = ['author_audit', 'post_audit']; public function up(Schema $schema): void { foreach (self::TABLES as $table) { $isV1 = (bool) $this->connection->fetchOne( "SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = current_schema() AND table_name = ? AND column_name = 'transaction_hash'", [$table], ); $this->abortIf( $isV1 && (bool) $this->connection->fetchOne(sprintf('SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM %s)', $table)), sprintf('%s holds v1 entries: run bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all first.', $table), ); $hash = md5($table); foreach (['transaction_hash', 'blame_id', 'object_id', 'discriminator'] as $index) { $this->addSql(sprintf('DROP INDEX IF EXISTS %s_%s_idx', $index, $hash)); } $this->addSql(sprintf( 'ALTER TABLE %s' .' ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS schema_version SMALLINT DEFAULT 2 NOT NULL,' .' ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS transaction_id CHAR(26) DEFAULT NULL,' .' ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS blame JSONB DEFAULT NULL,' .' DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS transaction_hash,' .' DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS blame_user,' .' DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS blame_user_fqdn,' .' DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS blame_user_firewall,' .' DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS ip,' .' ALTER schema_version SET DEFAULT 2,' .' ALTER id TYPE BIGINT,' .' ALTER type TYPE VARCHAR(11)', $table, )); $this->addSql(sprintf('CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS transaction_id_%s_idx ON %s (transaction_id)', $hash, $table)); $this->addSql(sprintf('CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS object_id_type_%s_idx ON %s (object_id, type)', $hash, $table)); $this->addSql(sprintf('CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS blame_id_created_at_%s_idx ON %s (blame_id, created_at)', $hash, $table)); } } public function down(Schema $schema): void { $this->throwIrreversibleMigrationException('The v1 audit schema can only be restored from a backup.'); } } On PostgreSQL, the (blame_user, blame_id) index of 1.x goes away with the blame_user column. When at least one entity declares an #[AuditRoot], generate the creation of the audit_root table as usual: it is a new, empty table. On MySQL, the same migration cannot rely on IF EXISTS: MySQL supports neither ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS nor DROP INDEX IF EXISTS (MariaDB does, but a migration that must also run on MySQL cannot rely on it). Introspect each table first ($this->connection->createSchemaManager()->introspectTable($table)) and add a statement only when hasColumn() or hasIndex() says it is needed; blame is a JSON column there. Drop the blame_user_blame_id_<md5>_idx index explicitly before the blame_user column: MySQL and MariaDB keep an index on the remaining columns of a multi-column index, under its legacy name. Compare the result with audit:schema:update --dump-sql on a copy. Then deploy in this order: Put the application in maintenance mode and stop writing audits (step 4). Deploy 2.0 with this migration, without running doctrine:migrations:migrate at start for this deployment: the migration would stop on the populated v1 tables, and the deployment with it. The other pending migrations of the release then run at item 4: make sure the code does not need them before. Run audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all (step 6). Run doctrine:migrations:migrate. On the migrated tables, it does what audit:schema:update does in step 7. Check and reopen (step 8): audit:schema:update --dump-sql has nothing left to do, and doctrine:migrations:diff generates nothing more for the audit tables. With #[AuditRoot], run audit:roots:rebuild first (step 4). Test and CI databases built from the migrations have empty audit tables: the migration brings them to v2 on its own.

# Preview the DDL (no writes) bin/console audit:schema:migrate --dump-sql --convert-all # Run the migration: new columns, transaction hash conversion, diffs conversion, then legacy columns dropped bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all Always pass --convert-all (or both --convert-transaction-hash and --convert-diffs): Command Result --force --convert-all Recommended. Every row reaches schema_version 2, transactions stay grouped (one ULID per legacy transaction_hash, across all tables), and the legacy columns are dropped. --force --convert-transaction-hash Transactions stay grouped; rows keep their legacy diffs (schema_version 1, still readable). Run --convert-diffs later to finish. --force --convert-diffs Diffs are converted; transaction_hash is kept so that --convert-transaction-hash can run later. The table stays a legacy table until then. --force alone New columns added, blame migrated; transaction_hash is kept and the diffs stay at schema_version 1. The table stays a legacy table until the conversions run. --force --drop-transaction-hash ⚠️ transaction_hash is dropped without conversion: legacy rows lose their transaction grouping for good. Only on request: this option cannot be combined with --convert-transaction-hash or --convert-all. The command migrates the audit tables of the entities currently configured as auditable, each on the storage its entity is mapped to. It holds a lock: a second run started meanwhile does nothing and exits with an error. The lock is local to the host: run the migration from a single host, not from every replica or pod of a deployment. A row whose diffs cannot be converted without losing or misreading them (not valid JSON, not an object, a field entry that is not an object, an unknown type) is left as it is, at schema_version 1, and listed at the end of the run, which then exits with an error. It stays readable as a legacy entry; fix or delete it, then run the command again. On large datasets, the conversions can run in several commands (--convert-transaction-hash, then --convert-diffs), or in chunks with --limit during the maintenance window: each run resumes where the previous one stopped, and the legacy columns are only dropped by a run without --limit.

bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql bin/console audit:schema:update --force This adds the indexes of the v2 schema (transaction_id, (object_id, type), (blame_id, created_at)), drops the object_id, blame_id and discriminator indexes of 1.x, and aligns the column types and defaults (id becomes a BIGINT, which rebuilds the table on MySQL and MariaDB and rewrites it on PostgreSQL). It is much shorter than the migration itself, about 20 seconds per million rows on MySQL 8.4 and 8 seconds on PostgreSQL 17 in a test container, but include it in the window.
documents.s: 7️⃣ Apply the rest of the v2 schema

documents.t: # Both must report that there is nothing left to do bin/console audit:schema:migrate bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql audit:schema:migrate without options exits with an error while a table still has a legacy column or rows with unconverted diffs (schema_version 1), and tells which. A run that only does a step of the migration (--limit, or a single conversion option) ends with "Step done. The migration is not complete" instead of the success message. Open a few audit entries (in the bundle's viewer, or through the Reader): the user, IP and transaction grouping of the migrated entries must be there. Then restart the workers and scheduled tasks, and leave maintenance mode. Optionally, reclaim the disk space used during the migration: OPTIMIZE TABLE on MySQL / MariaDB, VACUUM FULL on PostgreSQL (both lock the table while they run).

// Before (1.x) $entry->transactionHash; // SHA-1 VARCHAR(40) string // After (2.0) $entry->transactionId; // ULID CHAR(26) string See Breaking Changes for the other changes that may affect your code.

Reader and Query handle both schemas, but SQL written by hand against the audit tables does not: repositories that UNION several audit tables, reports, views, BI dashboards, Doctrine migrations or scripts. After audit:schema:migrate, any query naming transaction_hash, blame_user, blame_user_fqdn, blame_user_firewall or ip fails with an unknown column error. Search your code base (SQL strings, .sql files, views, migrations) for these names, and for paths into the diffs JSON, before the maintenance window. Columns​ 1.x 2.0, MySQL / MariaDB 2.0, PostgreSQL 2.0, SQLite transaction_hash transaction_id transaction_id transaction_id blame_user JSON_VALUE(blame, '$.username') blame->>'username' json_extract(blame, '$.username') blame_user_fqdn JSON_VALUE(blame, '$.user_fqdn') blame->>'user_fqdn' json_extract(blame, '$.user_fqdn') blame_user_firewall JSON_VALUE(blame, '$.user_firewall') blame->>'user_firewall' json_extract(blame, '$.user_firewall') ip JSON_VALUE(blame, '$.ip') blame->>'ip' json_extract(blame, '$.ip') blame_id, object_id, type, discriminator, extra_data, created_at unchanged unchanged unchanged transaction_id holds a ULID, not the SHA-1 of 1.x: the conversion gives one ULID per legacy hash across all audit tables, so joins and GROUP BY between audit tables keep working once the column is renamed. A transaction hash stored outside the audit tables (in your own tables, logs, URLs) no longer matches anything. blame is NULL when an entry has no blame at all (no user, no IP, no blame context). Otherwise each key is present, set to JSON null when unknown, so blame_user_firewall IS NOT NULL becomes JSON_VALUE(blame, '$.user_firewall') IS NOT NULL (MySQL / MariaDB). ⚠️ On MySQL, do not use blame->>'$.user_firewall' for a null test: on a JSON null it returns the string 'null', not SQL NULL, so IS NOT NULL is true for every row that has a blame. JSON_VALUE() (MySQL 8.0.21+, MariaDB) returns SQL NULL. MariaDB has no ->> operator. blame may also carry a via key (blame context, see Blame contexts). id becomes a BIGINT: a column or variable that stores an audit id in an INT must be widened. diffs​ Entry 1.x diffs 2.0 diffs insert / update {"field": {"old": …, "new": …}, …} (insert: plus @source) {"source": {…}, "changes": {"field": {"old": …, "new": …}}} remove {"class": …, "id": …, "label": …, "table": …} {"source": {"class", "id", "label", "table"}, "changes": {}} (changes filled with full_snapshot_on_remove) associate / dissociate {"source": …, "target": …, "is_owning_side": …, "table": "<join table>"} same, table renamed join_table A path into a field diff gets a changes level: MySQL / MariaDB PostgreSQL SQLite new value of email JSON_VALUE(diffs, '$.changes.email.new') diffs->'changes'->'email'->>'new' json_extract(diffs, '$.changes.email.new') email changed JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(diffs, 'one', '$.changes.email') diffs->'changes' ? 'email' json_type(diffs, '$.changes.email') IS NOT NULL WARNING A 1.x path does not fail, it finds nothing. diffs->'email' IS NOT NULL (PostgreSQL), JSON_EXTRACT(diffs, '$.email') (MySQL) or json_extract(diffs, '$.email') (SQLite) raise no error on a v2 row: they just never match, since the field is under changes. A query that expects rows returns none, and a query or a test that checks that no row matches still passes, but no longer checks anything. Look for these paths before the migration: an error will not point them out. A diffs LIKE '%"email"%' test still matches after the migration, but also matches the source block (its label) and fields of a JSON deep diff: prefer the paths above, or ChangedFieldFilter through the Reader. Until --convert-diffs has run on every row, a table holds both formats: rows with schema_version 1 keep the 1.x diffs. Filter on schema_version = 2, or handle both. diffs, blame and extra_data are native JSON on MySQL / MariaDB and JSONB on PostgreSQL (an INSERT needs a ::jsonb cast there); TEXT on SQLite. Example​ Entries of a user's HTTP requests (firewall known), grouped by transaction, on MySQL: -- Before (1.x) SELECT transaction_hash, MIN(created_at) FROM post_audit WHERE blame_id = :user AND blame_user_firewall IS NOT NULL GROUP BY transaction_hash; -- After (2.0) SELECT transaction_id, MIN(created_at) FROM post_audit WHERE blame_id = :user AND JSON_VALUE(blame, '$.user_firewall') IS NOT NULL GROUP BY transaction_id;

documents.t: The migration stopped in the middle (timeout, lost connection, Ctrl+C). Run the same command again. The added columns are kept, converted rows are skipped, transactions already given a ULID keep it, and the legacy columns are dropped last, so a new run completes the migration. On MySQL and MariaDB, DDL statements are not transactional: do not drop or restore anything by hand before the new run. If the run keeps failing, restore the backup and run it again after fixing the cause. audit:schema:update says that audit tables are still on the legacy v1 schema. audit:schema:migrate has not run, or not to the end (for example, only --convert-diffs ran, or a run used --limit). Run audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all. audit:schema:migrate reports nothing to migrate, but a v1 audit table is still there. Only the audit tables of the entities currently configured as auditable are migrated. A table left by an entity that is no longer audited is ignored: audit it again for the time of the migration, or keep its backup and drop it. "The command is already running in another process." Another audit:schema:migrate holds the lock on this host. Wait for it to finish. The lock does not cover other hosts: make sure only one host runs the migration. Some rows "could not be converted". Their diffs are not valid JSON, do not decode to an object, hold a field entry that is not an object, or their type is unknown: they were left as they are, at schema_version 1. Look at them with the ids listed by the command, fix or delete them, then run audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-diffs again. A Doctrine migration wants to change or drop the audit columns. It was generated against v1 audit tables: delete it, run audit:schema:migrate and audit:schema:update, then generate the migration again. If your audit tables are created by Doctrine migrations, write the migration described in Audit tables managed by Doctrine Migrations instead. Test or CI databases still have v1 audit tables after the upgrade. They are built by running the Doctrine migrations, which created the v1 tables, and audit:schema:migrate never ran on them. Add the migration described in Audit tables managed by Doctrine Migrations. audit:schema:update --dump-sql shows a change of transaction_id to CHAR(26). Development builds of 2.x created transaction_id as VARCHAR(26). Apply the change once: both audit:schema:update and doctrine:schema:update then agree. Disk full during the migration. Free some space, then run the command again: it resumes. Plan for up to 4 times the size of the audit tables on PostgreSQL.

Column (1.x) Column (2.0) Notes transaction_hash VARCHAR(40) transaction_id CHAR(26) SHA-1 replaced by ULID blame_user VARCHAR(255) (removed) Merged into blame JSON blame_user_fqdn VARCHAR(255) (removed) Merged into blame JSON blame_user_firewall VARCHAR(100) (removed) Merged into blame JSON ip VARCHAR(45) (removed) Merged into blame JSON (new) blame JSON NULL {"username","user_fqdn","user_firewall","ip"} (new) schema_version SMALLINT DEFAULT 2 1 = legacy diffs, 2 = v2 format (new or converted rows). audit:schema:migrate adds it with a default of 1, which marks the existing rows, and sets 2 when it drops the last legacy column (a table that keeps transaction_hash keeps 1 until then) Indexes: Index (1.x) Index (2.0) transaction_hash transaction_id (blame_user, blame_id) (added in 1.x for the viewer's user filter) (removed), the viewer reads blame_id object_id (removed), covered by (object_id, type) blame_id (removed), covered by (blame_id, created_at) discriminator (removed), always filtered along with object_id or created_at (object_id, type) (history of an object) (blame_id, created_at) (timeline of a user) audit:schema:migrate drops the 1.x indexes with their columns, and audit:schema:update creates the 2.0 ones and drops the object_id, blame_id and discriminator indexes: fewer indexes to maintain make each audit INSERT faster.
Property removed with no deprecated alias. Replace all reads with $entry->transactionId.

DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Attribute\Auditable, Ignore and Security, deprecated since 1.0, are removed. Import the attributes from the core: // Before (1.x) use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Attribute\Auditable; // After (2.0) use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable;

The interface of the Doctrine types whose value must be converted before it is audited is now DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Transaction\NeedsConversionToAuditableType. Its auditor 4.x counterpart, DH\Auditor\Transaction\NeedsConversionToAuditableType, is gone from auditor 5.0: a custom type implementing it must implement the provider's interface instead.

Custom providers must update any code reading the old flat keys from $event->getPayload(): Key (1.x) Key (2.0) Notes transaction_hash transaction_id ULID string blame_user blame → username Key of the blame JSON string blame_user_fqdn blame → user_fqdn Key of the blame JSON string blame_user_firewall blame → user_firewall Key of the blame JSON string ip blame → ip Key of the blame JSON string (new) schema_version 2 for all new entries blame, like diffs and extra_data, is a JSON string in the payload: json_decode($payload['blame'] ?? 'null', true)['username'] ?? null. Listeners that rewrite diffs​ A LifecycleEvent listener that changes $payload['diffs'] before the entry is written (to rewrite, add or remove field diffs) receives the v2 envelope, not the flat 1.x diff. It must: read and write the field diffs under changes; keep source (and, for an association, target, is_owning_side and join_table) as it is; when it replaces a JSON deep diff by an {old, new} diff, remove that field from deep_diffs, and drop deep_diffs once it is empty; leave the envelope of an association or a dissociation (no changes key) as it is: adding changes to it hides its structure. // Before (1.x) $diffs = json_decode($payload['diffs'], true); $diffs['tags'] = ['old' => $oldTags, 'new' => $newTags]; $payload['diffs'] = json_encode($diffs); // After (2.0) $envelope = json_decode($payload['diffs'], true); if (!\array_key_exists('changes', $envelope)) { return; // associate / dissociate: no field diffs } $envelope['changes']['tags'] = ['old' => $oldTags, 'new' => $newTags]; $envelope['deep_diffs'] = array_values(array_diff($envelope['deep_diffs'] ?? [], ['tags'])); if ([] === $envelope['deep_diffs']) { unset($envelope['deep_diffs']); } $payload['diffs'] = json_encode($envelope); $event->setPayload($payload); Nothing checks the envelope when the entry is written, and a wrong one is misread without any error: a v2 envelope without changes is returned whole by getDiffs(), like an association, so field diffs written next to source show source as a changed field, and without source the entry loses its summary (getDiffSource() returns null); a field left in deep_diffs is walked as a tree of changed keys (old, new).

For entries written with schema_version >= 2, getDiffs() returns the changes sub-array from the unified diffs envelope. Legacy v1 rows are unaffected. // schema_version = 1: raw ['field' => ['old' => x, 'new' => y], ...] // schema_version >= 2: envelope['changes'] — same shape $changes = $entry->getDiffs();

documents.t: In 1.x, Query::count() returned 0 when the query failed (missing audit table, lost connection, SQL error), while execute() on the same query threw. It now lets the exception through, like execute(). Code that worked around the silent 0 (for example by taking the larger of count() and the number of fetched entries) can drop it.
documents.s: Query::count() no longer hides database errors

documents.t: If any audit table still has a legacy column (transaction_hash, blame_user, blame_user_fqdn, blame_user_firewall or ip), audit:schema:update will refuse to run and print an error listing the affected tables. Run audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all first.
documents.s: audit:schema:update now guards against v1 tables

documents.t: In 1.x, the attributes of an #[Auditable] entity replaced its whole configured options (except retention): the entity ignored_columns given in the configuration (e.g. the bundle YAML) were silently dropped. They are now added to the #[Ignore] properties, as documented. Check that the properties listed there are really meant to be ignored.
documents.s: Configured ignored_columns of #[Auditable] entities are applied

documents.t: The extra_data_provider callable takes no argument: it is now called once per flush (and once per batch of audit:snapshot) instead of once per audit entry, and every entry of the flush gets its value. A provider that returned a different value on each call (a counter, a timestamp) now returns one value per flush; use a LifecycleEvent listener for a value that depends on the audited entity.

The filters of a Query used to be derived from the index definitions of the audit table, so that getSupportedFilters() also returned the __composite_object_id_type and __composite_blame_id_created_at pseudo-names, which never made a valid filter. It now returns id, type, object_id, discriminator, transaction_id, blame_id, created_at, json, diffs, transaction_hash, blame, root and cursor.
None of these features exists in 1.x, except the listener attachment by a container (also in 1.4). They are all optional: a 1.x configuration keeps working unchanged.

Feature Documentation Batch INSERT (batch_size): the audit entries of a transaction are written with multi-row INSERT statements, 10 to 67 % faster flushes with many entities Batch INSERT Per-entity retention: #[Auditable(maxAge: …, maxEntries: …)] or the max_age / max_entries entity options, applied by audit:clean Retention Policy Export with audit:export: NDJSON, JSON or CSV, streamed, filtered by entity, object, period or user, optionally anonymized audit:export Changed field filter (ChangedFieldFilter, changed_field query option): entries whose diff touches a field Filters Readable values in diffs with #[DiffLabel] and a DiffLabelResolverInterface service #[DiffLabel] Masked values with #[Mask]: the change of a field recorded as "***" or as an HMAC keyed with mask_secret #[Mask] JSON deep diffs: a JSON field change can be stored as a tree of the changed keys, listed under deep_diffs in the envelope (read with Entry::isDeepDiff()) Entry Full snapshot on remove (full_snapshot_on_remove): remove entries record the last value of every audited field Configuration Compression (compression): compressed diffs and extra_data columns on MariaDB Compression skip_disabled_entities: no audit table for entities disabled by default Skipping Disabled Entities Initial snapshot with audit:snapshot: an insert entry flagged as a snapshot records the state of the entities that existed before auditing started audit:snapshot Audited properties allowlist (audited_columns) and per-object ignored properties (ignored_columns_resolver) Ignored Properties Blame contexts: how a change was made (console command, import, message…) in the via key of the blame JSON Blame contexts Impersonator (switch user): an impersonator key in the blame JSON, read by $entry->impersonator and filtered by ImpersonatorFilter; user_fqdn is the class given by the user provider Filters Histories across tables: #[AuditRoot] and the audit_root index, Reader::createRootQuery() with cursor pagination, getLastChanges(), getFieldHistory(), BlameOriginFilter, audit:roots:rebuild Histories Pages of transactions: Query::transactions() / countTransactions() (and transactionsOf() / countTransactionsOf() across tables), Query::transactionEntries(), Query::countTransactionsByDay(), RootQuery::fetchTransactions() / countTransactions(): pages of whole actions instead of entries Pages of transactions New indexes (object_id, type) and (blame_id, created_at), for the history of an object and the timeline of a user, and a lighter flush pipeline Performance

user_fqdn is the fqdn of the user returned by the user provider (the class of the user in the application), no longer the class of that object, which was DH\Auditor\User\User whenever the built-in class was used: null when the user provider gives none. When that user has an impersonator (switch user), the blame JSON gets an impersonator key, {"id": "1", "username": "admin", "fqdn": "App\\Entity\\Admin"}, read by $entry->impersonator and filtered by ImpersonatorFilter (see Filters).

The blame context current when the entities are flushed (see the core Blame Context page) is written in the via key of the blame JSON: {"type": "import", "label": "Import batch #42"}. It is captured at flush time, so it still applies when the database transaction is committed after the context was popped. A context carrying a user blames that user (blame_id, username, user_fqdn) instead of the user provider's one.
$source = $entry->getDiffSource(); // ['id' => '42', 'class' => 'App\Entity\Post', 'label' => 'My post', 'table' => 'post'] // Returns null for schema_version = 1 entries.
$target = $entry->getDiffTarget(); // ['id' => '7', 'class' => 'App\Entity\Tag', 'label' => 'PHP', 'table' => 'tag'] // Returns null for non-association entries or schema_version = 1.

When auditing is enabled on a database that already holds data, the history of an entity used to start at its first change. audit:snapshot writes one insert entry flagged with "snapshot": true per existing entity, in batches, and skips the entities that already have an audit history: php bin/console audit:snapshot --all Entry::isSnapshot() (auditor 5.0) tells these entries from real insertions. See Schema Management.

documents.t: The Reader automatically adapts queries to use transaction_id or transaction_hash depending on which column exists in each table. Mixed environments (some tables migrated, some not) are fully supported.

The audited_columns entity option audits only the listed properties (an allowlist, instead of ignoring all the others). The ignored_columns_resolver option takes a callable (see IgnoredColumnsResolverInterface) that returns the properties to ignore for a given entity object. Ignoring always wins over the allowlist. See Configuration.

disableListenerAttachment() leaves the Doctrine listeners to a dependency injection container, which declares getDoctrineSubscriber() as a lazy listener: flushes made before the provider is built are audited (auditor-bundle does it). One subscriber is now shared by all the auditing entity managers: auditing entity managers sharing an event manager no longer write each audit entry twice. Also in 1.4. See Services.

The main entry point for the library. namespace DH\Auditor; final class Auditor { public function __construct( Configuration $configuration, EventDispatcherInterface $dispatcher, bool $registerAuditEventSubscriber = true, ); public function getEventDispatcher(): EventDispatcherInterface; public function getConfiguration(): Configuration; // Provider management public function getProviders(): array; public function getProvider(string $name): ProviderInterface; public function hasProvider(string $name): bool; public function registerProvider(ProviderInterface $provider): self; // Storage control public function enableStorage(ProviderInterface $provider): self; public function disableStorage(ProviderInterface $provider): self; public function isStorageEnabled(ProviderInterface $provider): bool; // Auditing control public function enableAuditing(ProviderInterface $provider): self; public function disableAuditing(ProviderInterface $provider): self; public function isAuditingEnabled(ProviderInterface $provider): bool; } disableStorage() stops AuditEventSubscriber from passing audit entries to that provider's persist(); disableAuditing() tells the provider to stop producing entries (the Doctrine provider checks isAuditingEnabled(), a custom auditing provider must do the same). Both refuse to switch off the last enabled provider of their role, and disabling a provider that is already disabled does nothing. The six methods throw an InvalidArgumentException for a provider that was not registered with registerProvider(). By default, the constructor attaches AuditEventSubscriber to $dispatcher (priority AuditEventSubscriber::PRIORITY, i.e. -1_000_000). Pass false as third argument when the subscriber is declared as a listener of the dispatcher instead, e.g. in a Symfony container: since Symfony 8.2, the compiled event dispatcher deprecates addListener() at runtime.

namespace DH\Auditor\Attribute; #[\Attribute(\Attribute::TARGET_CLASS)] class Auditable { public function __construct( public bool $enabled = true, public ?string $maxAge = null, // ISO 8601 duration, e.g. 'P1Y' public ?int $maxEntries = null, // keep the N most recent entries ); public function getRetentionPolicy(): RetentionPolicy; } maxAge and maxEntries define an optional retention policy, applied by providers that support pruning (audit:clean with the Doctrine provider). Invalid values throw DH\Auditor\Exception\InvalidArgumentException when the attribute is instantiated.

namespace DH\Auditor\Model; final readonly class RetentionPolicy { public function __construct(public ?string $maxAge = null, public ?int $maxEntries = null); public function isEmpty(): bool; // Date before which entries are eligible for deletion, null when no max age is set public function getCutoff(\DateTimeImmutable $now): ?\DateTimeImmutable; } Validation rules: maxAge must be an ISO 8601 duration greater than zero (P0D is rejected), maxEntries must be a positive integer.

namespace DH\Auditor\Attribute; #[\Attribute(\Attribute::TARGET_PROPERTY | \Attribute::TARGET_CLASS | \Attribute::IS_REPEATABLE)] class Ignore { public function __construct(public ?string $field = null); } On a property, the property is the ignored field: leave field out. On a class, field names the ignored field, and the attribute can be repeated. This is the form to use on models that do not declare a property per column, such as Eloquent models: use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable; use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Ignore; #[Auditable] #[Ignore(field: 'password')] #[Ignore(field: 'remember_token')] class User extends Model {}

See Histories.

namespace DH\Auditor\Attribute; #[\Attribute(\Attribute::TARGET_PROPERTY | \Attribute::TARGET_CLASS | \Attribute::IS_REPEATABLE)] class DiffLabel { public function __construct(public string $resolver, public ?string $field = null); } Annotates a field with a resolver service that will translate the raw stored value into a human-readable label. The resolver argument must be the FQCN of a service that implements DiffLabelResolverInterface. The label is stored alongside the raw value in the JSON diff as {"value": x, "label": "y"}, consistent with how relation fields already store {id, label, class, table}. Example: use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable; use DH\Auditor\Attribute\DiffLabel; #[Auditable] class Order { #[DiffLabel(resolver: StatusLabelResolver::class)] private int $status; } As with #[Ignore], the attribute can also be put on the class, repeated, with field naming the field: #[DiffLabel(resolver: StatusLabelResolver::class, field: 'status')].

namespace DH\Auditor\Attribute; use DH\Auditor\Masking\MaskStrategy; #[\Attribute(\Attribute::TARGET_PROPERTY | \Attribute::TARGET_CLASS | \Attribute::IS_REPEATABLE)] class Mask { public function __construct(public MaskStrategy $strategy = MaskStrategy::Hidden, public ?string $field = null); } Records that a field changed without storing its values. Unlike #[Ignore], the change still shows in the history. Strategy Stored value MaskStrategy::Hidden "***" (Masker::HIDDEN_VALUE) MaskStrategy::KeyedHash HMAC-SHA256 of the value, keyed with the mask secret of the provider A null value stays null. With KeyedHash, equal values give equal hashes, so the entries of one value can be found without storing it; changing the secret changes the hashes recorded from then on. use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable; use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Mask; use DH\Auditor\Masking\MaskStrategy; #[Auditable] class User { #[Mask(strategy: MaskStrategy::KeyedHash)] private string $email; #[Mask] private string $pin; } As with #[Ignore], the attribute can also be put on the class, repeated, with field naming the field: #[Mask(field: 'email')]. WARNING Only the values of the field in the diffs are masked. A value written elsewhere is not, in particular the label of the entity (its __toString() or a label resolver), recorded in the source of every entry. Providers replace the values through DH\Auditor\Masking\Masker: namespace DH\Auditor\Masking; final readonly class Masker { public const string HIDDEN_VALUE = '***'; public function __construct(?string $secret = null); // null stays null; a string is hashed as is, any other value as its JSON encoding public function mask(MaskStrategy $strategy, mixed $value): ?string; }

namespace DH\Auditor\Contract; interface DiffLabelResolverInterface { /** * Resolves a raw audit diff value to a human-readable label. * * Called at write-time (during flush). Implementations MUST NOT flush the * same EntityManager or rely on an open transaction. A separate read-only * connection or a pure in-memory lookup is safe. * * Return null to fall back to storing the plain raw value without a label. */ public function __invoke(mixed $value): ?string; } Example implementation: use DH\Auditor\Contract\DiffLabelResolverInterface; final class StatusLabelResolver implements DiffLabelResolverInterface { private const LABELS = [ 1 => 'Pending', 2 => 'Processing', 3 => 'Shipped', 4 => 'Delivered', ]; public function __invoke(mixed $value): ?string { return self::LABELS[(int) $value] ?? null; } }

namespace DH\Auditor\Contract; interface EntityLabelResolverInterface { public function __invoke(object $entity): ?string; // label of "source" / "target", null = default } interface FieldLabelResolverInterface { public function resolve(string $entity, string $field): string; }

Manage audit data via the command line NOTE These commands are provided by auditor-doctrine-provider (not auditor core). For programmatic usage and standalone registration, see Schema Management. When using auditor-bundle or the standalone auditor-doctrine-provider, these console commands are available:

Command Description audit:schema:update Create or update audit tables to the current schema audit:schema:migrate Migrate legacy v1 audit tables to schema v2 audit:clean Remove old audit entries audit:snapshot Record the current state of existing entities audit:export Export audit entries as NDJSON, JSON or CSV audit:roots:rebuild Index existing entries under their audit roots
Creates new audit tables and updates existing ones to match the current schema.
Option Short Description --dump-sql Show SQL statements without executing them --force -f Execute the SQL statements

# Preview the SQL that would be executed php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql # Output: # The following SQL statements will be executed: # # CREATE TABLE users_audit (...); # CREATE INDEX idx_type_xxx ON users_audit (type); # ... # Execute the changes php bin/console audit:schema:update --force # Both: show SQL and execute php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql --force

Run this command: After adding #[Auditable] to a new entity After updating auditor to a new version During deployment to ensure schema is up-to-date TIP The command is safe to run multiple times. Existing tables are updated (not recreated), existing data is preserved, and only necessary changes are applied.
Code Meaning 0 Success (including "nothing to update") 1 Error or missing required options

Migrates legacy v1 audit tables to schema v2 (ULID transaction_id, unified blame JSON column). Safe to run multiple times; skips already-migrated tables. CAUTION audit:schema:update refuses to run while any audit table still has the legacy v1 schema. Always run audit:schema:migrate --force first when upgrading from auditor-bundle 7.x or earlier.

Option Description --dump-sql Show SQL statements without executing them --force, -f Execute the migration --convert-all Convert transaction hashes and diffs in one pass (recommended) --convert-transaction-hash Convert SHA-1 transaction_hash values to ULID format --convert-diffs Convert legacy diffs JSON to the v2 envelope format --limit=N Convert N transactions or rows only, keep the legacy columns (resumable), print an estimate of the remaining time --drop-transaction-hash ⚠️ Drop transaction_hash without converting it: legacy rows lose their transaction grouping for good

# Preview the DDL that would be executed php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --dump-sql # Full migration in one pass (recommended) php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all # Estimate the duration on a copy of the production data php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all --limit=10000
Removes audit entries older than a specified retention period.
Argument Default Description keep P12M Retention period as ISO 8601 duration

Option Short Description --no-confirm Skip confirmation prompt --dry-run Show what would be deleted without executing --dump-sql Show the SQL statements --date -d Clean audits before a specific date --exclude -x Exclude specific entities (can be used multiple times) --include -i Include only specific entities (can be used multiple times)
The keep argument uses ISO 8601 duration format: Format Meaning P12M 12 months P1Y 1 year P6M 6 months P30D 30 days P7D 7 days P1D 1 day PT12H 12 hours

An entity can define its own retention policy, either with #[Auditable] or in the bundle configuration (see the auditor-bundle documentation): use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable; #[Auditable(maxAge: 'P7Y')] // keep 7 years of history class Payment {} #[Auditable(maxEntries: 10_000)] // keep the 10,000 most recent entries class Session {} #[Auditable(maxAge: 'P1Y', maxEntries: 500)] class User {} maxAge is an ISO 8601 duration greater than zero; maxEntries is a positive integer. Invalid values make the attribute fail as soon as it is loaded. For an entity with a maxAge, that value replaces the global cutoff (keep argument or --date option), whether it is shorter or longer. Entities without a maxAge keep using the global cutoff, exactly as before. maxEntries applies on top of the age rule: an entry is deleted when it is older than the cutoff or not among the maxEntries most recent entries of the entity (most recent first, ties broken by insertion order). With single-table inheritance, the classes of a hierarchy share one audit table: each rule only deletes the entries of its own class (discriminator column). Entries without a discriminator are left untouched. Every policy is validated before anything is deleted: one invalid policy makes the command fail without deleting anything. Cutoffs are computed in the auditor timezone (the one audit entries are written in). The policies in use are listed before the confirmation prompt: Per-entity retention policies (they override the global cutoff for these entities): --------------------- --------- ------------- Entity Max age Max entries --------------------- --------- ------------- App\Entity\Payment P7Y - App\Entity\Session - 10000 --------------------- --------- -------------

Basic Cleanup​ # Keep last 12 months (default) php bin/console audit:clean # Keep last 6 months php bin/console audit:clean P6M # Keep last 30 days php bin/console audit:clean P30D Preview Mode​ # See what would be deleted without actually deleting php bin/console audit:clean P6M --dry-run # See the SQL statements php bin/console audit:clean P6M --dump-sql Non-Interactive​ # Skip confirmation (useful for cron jobs) php bin/console audit:clean P12M --no-confirm Custom Date​ # Delete audits before a specific date php bin/console audit:clean --date=2024-01-01 # Combine with no-confirm for scripts php bin/console audit:clean --date=2023-12-31 --no-confirm Entity Filtering​ # Exclude specific entities from cleanup php bin/console audit:clean -x App\\Entity\\User -x App\\Entity\\Payment # Include only specific entities php bin/console audit:clean -i App\\Entity\\Log -i App\\Entity\\Session # Long form php bin/console audit:clean --exclude=App\\Entity\\User --include=App\\Entity\\Post

You are about to clean audits created before 2024-01-15 14:30:45: 12 classes involved. Do you want to proceed? (yes/no) [no]: > yes Starting... Cleaning audit tables... (users_audit) 12/12 [============================] 100% Cleaning audit tables... (done) [OK] Success.

For automated cleanup, add to your crontab: # Clean up audits older than 12 months, daily at 2 AM 0 2 * * * /path/to/php /path/to/bin/console audit:clean P12M --no-confirm >> /var/log/audit-clean.log 2>&1 With auditor-bundle, pruning can also be scheduled with Symfony Scheduler (opt-in, see the bundle configuration). Unlike audit:clean, a scheduled run only applies explicit retention policies: entities without a policy are left untouched unless a default max age is configured. TIP Use Symfony Messenger Scheduler if available for more robust scheduling.
Code Meaning 0 Success or cancelled by user 1 Error

Records the current state of existing entities in their audit tables. Run it once auditing is enabled on a database that already holds data: the history of each entity then starts with its state at that time instead of its first change.
Argument Description entities Audited entities to snapshot (FQCN), or --all

Option Short Default Description --all -a Snapshot every audited entity --batch-size -b 500 Entities read and written per database transaction --force -f Also snapshot entities that already have an audit history --dry-run Count the entities to snapshot, write nothing

One insert entry per entity, whose diffs carry "snapshot": true (Entry::isSnapshot() returns true): every audited field with old: null and its current value as new, as for an insertion. Its created_at is the date of the snapshot and its blame is the console user. Entities that already have an audit entry are skipped, so the command can be run again safely. To-many associations are not snapshotted, and enabled Doctrine filters (e.g. soft-delete) apply.

# Preview: how many entities would be snapshotted php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --dry-run # Snapshot two entities php bin/console audit:snapshot 'App\Entity\Post' 'App\Entity\Author' # Snapshot everything with bigger batches php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --batch-size=2000
Code Meaning 0 Success (or already running) 1 Error (e.g. entity not audited) 2 Invalid arguments

Exports audit entries as NDJSON (default, recommended for large exports), JSON or CSV, streamed to the standard output or to a file. Each line or row is an Entry::toArray(). php bin/console audit:export [options] [entity] Option Description entity Entity FQCN to export, all auditable entities by default --id Filter by object ID --from Entries created on or after this date (ISO 8601) --to Entries created on or before this date (ISO 8601) --blame-id Filter by user ID --format ndjson (default), json or csv --anonymize Mask the user and IP fields --output Write to this file instead of the standard output php bin/console audit:export App\\Entity\\Post --format=csv --from=2026-01-01 --output=posts.csv

Indexes the existing audit entries under their audit roots (#[AuditRoot]), after declaring a new root or after migrating audit tables to schema v2. Only missing index rows are written, so the command can be run again. php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild [--entity=FQCN ...] [--dry-run] See Histories and the Doctrine provider history page.

These commands use Symfony's Lock component to prevent concurrent execution: The command is already running in another process. NOTE This ensures data integrity when running commands in parallel or from cron jobs.

Always preview first - Use --dump-sql and --dry-run before executing Backup before cleanup - Especially for large deletions Schedule regular cleanups - Prevent unlimited growth Monitor disk space - Audit tables can grow quickly Consider retention policies - Different entities may need different retention Test in staging - Verify commands work as expected before production
WARNING Wait for the other instance to finish, or check for stuck processes.
NOTE This means your audit tables are already up-to-date.
IMPORTANT Ensure the database user has CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE permissions.
For very large tables, consider: Running during off-peak hours Increasing PHP timeout Breaking into smaller date ranges

Since auditor 5.0, damienharper/auditor contains no Doctrine code. DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\… classes come from damienharper/auditor-doctrine-provider; Symfony applications install damienharper/auditor-bundle, which requires it. See Which packages do I need?.

// ❌ $entry->extraData is already an array (or null) $data = json_decode($entry->extraData, true); // ✅ $data = $entry->extraData ?? []; The same holds for $entry->blame, already decoded, and getDiffs(), which returns an array.

The payload of a LifecycleEvent carries the operation in type, as a string: // ❌ there is no 'action' key $operation = $event->getPayload()['action']; // ✅ $operation = $event->getPayload()['type']; // 'insert', 'update', 'remove', 'associate', 'dissociate'

The Doctrine provider audits the changes flushed through the Doctrine ORM unit of work. Bulk DQL UPDATE/DELETE queries and raw SQL statements bypass it and are not recorded.

documents.t: #[Ignore] drops the field from the audit: its changes are not recorded at all. To record that a sensitive field changed without storing its values, use #[Mask] ("***", or an HMAC with MaskStrategy::KeyedHash, which needs the provider's mask secret). Only the values in the diffs are masked: the label of the entity (its __toString() or a label resolver) is stored in clear in every entry, so never build it from a masked field.

All configuration options available in auditor This section covers all configuration options available in auditor.

The main Configuration class accepts the following options: <?php use DH\Auditor\Configuration; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'enabled' => true, 'timezone' => 'UTC', 'user_provider' => null, 'security_provider' => null, 'role_checker' => null, 'extra_data_provider' => null, ]);

Option Type Default Description enabled bool true Enable or disable auditing globally timezone string 'UTC' Timezone used for audit timestamps user_provider callable|null null Callback that returns the current user security_provider callable|null null Callback that returns security context info role_checker callable|null null Callback that checks if user can view entity audits extra_data_provider callable|null null Callback that returns the extra_data of the entries of a flush (see Extra Data)
// Disable auditing $configuration->disable(); // Re-enable auditing $configuration->enable(); // Check if auditing is enabled if ($configuration->enabled) { // ... }

The user provider is a callable that returns information about the current user. This is used to record who made each change. use DH\Auditor\User\User; $configuration->setUserProvider(function (): ?User { // Return null if no user is authenticated $currentUser = $this->security->getUser(); if (null === $currentUser) { return null; } return new User( (string) $currentUser->getId(), // User identifier $currentUser->getUsername(), // Username for display $currentUser::class, // Class of the user (user_fqdn) ); }); The User class implements UserInterface: namespace DH\Auditor\User; interface UserInterface { public ?string $identifier { get; } public ?string $username { get; } public ?string $fqdn { get; } public ?UserInterface $impersonator { get; } } See User Provider Configuration for more details. To record how a change was made (an import, a command, a message…), see Blame Context.

The security provider returns the client IP address and the firewall name, as a list of two values: $configuration->setSecurityProvider(function (): array { return [ $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] ?? null, // client IP $this->getFirewallName(), // firewall name ]; }); See Security Provider Configuration for more details.

The role checker determines whether a user can view audits for a specific entity: $configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope): bool { // $entity is the FQCN of the audited entity // $scope is the action (e.g., 'view') // Example: Only admins can view User audits if ($entity === User::class) { return $this->security->isGranted('ROLE_ADMIN'); } // Allow everyone to view other audits return true; }); See Role Checker Configuration for more details.
The DoctrineProvider has its own configuration. See DoctrineProvider Configuration for details.

<?php use DH\Auditor\Auditor; use DH\Auditor\Configuration; use DH\Auditor\User\User; use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\EventDispatcher; $configuration = new Configuration([ 'enabled' => true, 'timezone' => 'Europe/Paris', ]); // Set user provider $configuration->setUserProvider(function (): ?User { $user = $securityContext->getUser(); if (null === $user) { return null; } return new User((string) $user->getId(), $user->getUsername(), $user::class); }); // Set security provider $configuration->setSecurityProvider(function (): array { return [$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] ?? null, null]; }); // Set role checker $configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope): bool { return $this->authorizationChecker->isGranted('ROLE_AUDIT_VIEWER'); }); $auditor = new Auditor($configuration, new EventDispatcher());
